# Compactifications {#sec-vi-compactifications}

Parts III to V chose the internal space for its isometries: the circle of Kaluza-Klein theory gives a $U(1)$ gauge
field and its tower of massive modes (@sec-kk-tower), a sphere or a group manifold gives non-abelian gauge fields
(Part IV), and coset space dimensional reduction (CSDR, Part V) makes the internal components of a higher-dimensional
gauge field into Higgs fields whose potential is fixed by the geometry. This chapter surveys compactifications chosen
for a different purpose, for what they leave behind at low energies: the amount of supersymmetry, the number of chiral
generations, the values of the moduli, and the hierarchy between the Planck scale and the electroweak scale. The three
sections follow the three main ideas. Special holonomy asks the internal manifold to admit parallel spinors, which
leads to Calabi-Yau threefolds, $G_2$ manifolds and their singular limits, the orbifolds, and to the nearly-Kähler
coset spaces in which CSDR and the supersymmetric compactifications meet. Flux compactifications thread the cycles of
the internal space with quantised field strengths, whose energy gives the moduli a potential and fixes them, and whose
many integer choices make the landscape of vacua. Warped and large extra dimensions give up the product structure of
spacetime or the smallness of the internal space, and explain the weakness of gravity by an exponential warp factor
(Randall-Sundrum) or by a large volume (Arkani-Hamed, Dimopoulos and Dvali). The chapter is a survey: the
higher-dimensional supergravity and string theory behind each construction are cited, not derived. One computation
per idea is carried out exactly in Sage: the Hodge numbers and Euler numbers that count generations, the Dirac
quantisation of a flux and the minimum of the potential it produces, and the warped solution of the five-dimensional
Einstein equations with the hierarchy and the localised graviton it implies. Every statement is followed by three
examples and three exercises with hidden solutions. A fourth section, @sec-compactification-fermions, derives the
fermion spectra of these compactifications, the families that the Euler numbers count, from the Dirac operators of
@sec-spinors-dirac-operator.

## Special holonomy: Calabi-Yau, G2, nearly-Kähler, orbifolds {#sec-vi-special-holonomy}

A compactification on $M_4 \times X$ preserves supersymmetry when the internal manifold $X$ admits spinors that are
constant in the sense of its Levi-Civita connection. Whether such spinors exist is decided by the holonomy group of $X$,
the group of rotations produced by parallel transport around closed loops. This section defines holonomy, states the
link with unbroken supersymmetry, and then meets the manifolds of reduced holonomy that string and M-theory use:
Calabi-Yau threefolds with their Hodge numbers, $G_2$ manifolds, the nearly-Kähler coset spaces of CSDR, and toroidal
orbifolds. The section ends by counting generations through Euler numbers.

### Holonomy and supersymmetry

Parallel transport along a curve maps tangent vectors at its start to tangent vectors at its end, preserving lengths and
angles (@def-parallel-transport). Along a closed loop it returns a rotation of the tangent space at the base point, and
the rotations obtained from all loops form a group.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcp-holonomy-group}
#### Holonomy group

Let $(X, g)$ be a connected Riemannian manifold of dimension $n$ and $p \in X$. For every piecewise smooth loop $\gamma$
based at $p$, parallel transport with the Levi-Civita connection gives an orthogonal map $P_\gamma : T_pX \to T_pX$.
These maps form a subgroup
$$
\operatorname{Hol}_p(g) = \{P_\gamma : \gamma \text{ a loop at } p\} \subset O(n),
$$ {#eq-vcp-holonomy}
the **holonomy group** of $g$; it lies in $SO(n)$ when $X$ is orientable, and the groups at different points are
conjugate. A connected, simply connected, irreducible and non-symmetric $X$ has holonomy $SO(n)$, $U(m)$ or $SU(m)$
($n = 2m$), $Sp(m)$ or $Sp(m)Sp(1)$ ($n = 4m$), $G_2$ ($n = 7$) or $Spin(7)$ ($n = 8$): **Berger's list**
[@acharya2004, Sec. 2.1 and Table 1].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The first example is the trivial case. On a flat torus parallel transport is the identity in the standard coordinates,
so no loop rotates anything.

::: {#exm-vcp-holonomy-torus}
#### The flat torus

On $T^n = \mathbb{R}^n/\mathbb{Z}^n$ with the flat metric the Christoffel symbols vanish, parallel vector fields are the
constant ones, and every $P_\gamma$ is the identity: $\operatorname{Hol}(T^n) = \{1\}$. The torus reductions of
@sec-vi-torus-scherk-schwarz owe their maximal supersymmetry to this.
:::

On the round sphere a loop does rotate vectors, by an angle equal to the enclosed area. All angles occur, so the
holonomy is the whole rotation group of the tangent plane.

::: {#exm-vcp-holonomy-sphere}
#### The two-sphere

Transport around the circle of latitude $\theta = \theta_0$ on the unit sphere rotates a vector by $2\pi(1 - \cos\theta_0)$,
the area of the enclosed cap (@exm-gauss-holonomy, @exr-vcp-holonomy-latitude). As $\theta_0$ runs over $(0, \pi)$ every
angle occurs, so $\operatorname{Hol}(S^2) = SO(2)$, the generic holonomy in two dimensions.
:::

A complex structure that is parallel restricts the holonomy further. For a Kähler manifold the holonomy must commute
with it, which cuts $SO(2m)$ down to the unitary group.

::: {#exm-vcp-holonomy-kahler}
#### Kähler manifolds

On a Kähler manifold of complex dimension $m$ the complex structure $J$ is parallel, so every $P_\gamma$ commutes with
$J$: holomorphic and antiholomorphic components of a vector do not mix under transport, and $\operatorname{Hol} \subset
U(m) \subset SO(2m)$ [@greene1997, Sec. 2.8]. The complex projective spaces $\mathbb{CP}^m$ with the Fubini-Study metric
have holonomy exactly $U(m)$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes the transport around a circle of latitude with Sage. It turns the statement of
@exm-vcp-holonomy-sphere into a linear differential equation whose solution is a rotation.

::: {#exr-vcp-holonomy-latitude}
#### Transport around a latitude

On the unit sphere, write the parallel transport equations along $\gamma(t) = (\theta_0, t)$, $0 \le t \le 2\pi$, solve them
with Sage, and show that one loop rotates every vector by $-2\pi\cos\theta_0$, which equals the enclosed area modulo
$2\pi$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\Gamma^\theta_{\varphi\varphi} = -\sin\theta\cos\theta$ and $\Gamma^\varphi_{\theta\varphi} = \cot\theta$ the equations
$\dot V^r = -\Gamma^r_{\varphi s}V^s$ read, in the orthonormal components $a = V^\theta$, $b = \sin\theta_0\,V^\varphi$, $\dot a
= \cos\theta_0\,b$, $\dot b = -\cos\theta_0\,a$: a rotation at angular speed $\cos\theta_0$. After $t = 2\pi$ the angle is
$-2\pi\cos\theta_0 = 2\pi(1 - \cos\theta_0) - 2\pi$:

{{< sage exr-vcp-holonomy-latitude >}}
:::

A cone is flat away from its apex, yet a loop around the apex rotates vectors. The second exercise separates the
holonomy from the restricted holonomy of contractible loops.

::: {#exr-vcp-holonomy-cone}
#### The cone

Cut a wedge of angle $\beta$ out of the plane and glue the edges to make a cone. Find the holonomy of a loop around the
apex and of a loop that does not enclose it. Which loops are contractible on the cone with its apex removed?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Away from the apex the cone is flat, so a loop that does not enclose the apex bounds a flat disc and has trivial
holonomy. Unrolling a loop around the apex onto the plane, a vector transported once around comes back to the cut and is
compared with itself across the glued edges, which meet at the angle $\beta$: it is rotated by $\beta$. The loops around
the apex are not contractible once the apex is removed, so the holonomy group is the cyclic group generated by the
rotation by $\beta$ while the restricted holonomy (contractible loops) is trivial. Orbifold singularities
(@def-vcp-toroidal-orbifold) are cones of this kind, with $\beta = 2\pi(1 - 1/m)$.
:::

Holonomy behaves simply under products: transport on $X_1 \times X_2$ acts on each factor separately. The third
exercise uses this to read off the holonomy of some product spaces.

::: {#exr-vcp-holonomy-product}
#### Products

Show that $\operatorname{Hol}(X_1 \times X_2) \subset \operatorname{Hol}(X_1) \times \operatorname{Hol}(X_2)$ for the product
metric, and find the holonomy of $S^2 \times S^2$, of $T^2 \times S^2$ and of $T^2 \times K3$, where the K3 surface has
holonomy $SU(2)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Levi-Civita connection of a product metric is the sum of the two connections, with no mixed Christoffel symbols, so
a loop $(\gamma_1, \gamma_2)$ is transported by $P_{\gamma_1} \oplus P_{\gamma_2}$ on $T_{p_1}X_1 \oplus T_{p_2}X_2$; taking
$\gamma_2$ constant shows that the product is all of $\operatorname{Hol}(X_1) \times \operatorname{Hol}(X_2)$. Hence
$\operatorname{Hol}(S^2 \times S^2) = SO(2) \times SO(2)$, $\operatorname{Hol}(T^2 \times S^2) = SO(2)$ acting on the sphere
factor, and $\operatorname{Hol}(T^2 \times K3) = SU(2) \subset SU(3)$: a Ricci-flat Kähler threefold whose holonomy is
smaller than $SU(3)$, and which therefore preserves more supersymmetry than a Calabi-Yau threefold.
:::
::::

Supersymmetry enters through the gravitino. In a background in which only the metric is non-zero, its variation is
the covariant derivative of the supersymmetry parameter, and an unbroken supersymmetry is a parallel spinor on the
internal space.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-vcp-parallel-spinors}
#### Parallel spinors and unbroken supersymmetry

In a compactification $M_d \times X$ of eleven-dimensional supergravity, or of ten-dimensional supergravity, in which
all fields but the metric vanish, the Killing spinor equation of @def-sugra11-transformation reduces on $X$ to
$$
\nabla_m\xi = 0 ,
$$ {#eq-vcp-parallel-spinor}
and the unbroken supersymmetries are counted by the parallel spinors $\xi$ of $X$. A parallel spinor is invariant under
the holonomy group acting in the spinor representation, so it exists only if $\operatorname{Hol}(X)$ is a proper
subgroup of $SO(n)$; a manifold with a parallel spinor is Ricci-flat, so $M_d \times X$ with $M_d$ flat solves the
vacuum Einstein equations. The fraction of the supercharges preserved is $1$ for the torus, $\tfrac14$ for holonomy
$SU(3)$ ($n = 6$), $\tfrac18$ for $G_2$ ($n = 7$) and $\tfrac1{16}$ for $Spin(7)$ ($n = 8$) [@acharya2004, Sec. 2.2,
eq. 2.10 and Table 2]. Quoted, with the spinor counting for $SU(3)$ checked in @exr-vcp-spinor-count.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The counting of invariant spinors is representation theory: decompose the spinor of $SO(n)$ under the holonomy group
and count singlets. The three examples do this for the three cases that matter most.

::: {#exm-vcp-spinor-su3}
#### $SU(3)$ holonomy

$SO(6)$ is locally $SU(4)$, and its two chiral spinors are the $\mathbf 4$ and $\bar{\mathbf 4}$. Under $SU(3) \subset
SU(4)$, $\mathbf 4 = \mathbf 3 + \mathbf 1$: one invariant spinor of each chirality, two of the eight spinor
components, the fraction $\tfrac14$. Type II strings on a Calabi-Yau threefold keep $8$ of $32$ supercharges ($N = 2$ in
four dimensions), the heterotic string $4$ of $16$ ($N = 1$).
:::

Seven dimensions have no chirality, and the spinor of $Spin(7)$ is real of dimension $8$. The exceptional group $G_2$
fixes exactly one direction in it.

::: {#exm-vcp-spinor-g2}
#### $G_2$ holonomy

Under $G_2 \subset Spin(7)$ the spinor decomposes as $\mathbf 8 = \mathbf 7 + \mathbf 1$ [@acharya2004, Sec. 2.2]: one
parallel spinor, the fraction $\tfrac18$. M-theory on a $G_2$ manifold keeps $4$ of $32$ supercharges, $N = 1$ in four
dimensions, the same amount as the heterotic string on a Calabi-Yau threefold [@acharya2004, Sec. 2.2].
:::

In four real dimensions holonomy $SU(2)$ is the Calabi-Yau condition for a complex surface. Because $SO(4)$ splits
into two $SU(2)$ factors, the count is particularly transparent.

::: {#exm-vcp-spinor-k3}
#### The K3 surface

$SO(4)$ is locally $SU(2) \times SU(2)$ and its chiral spinors are $(\mathbf 2, \mathbf 1)$ and $(\mathbf 1, \mathbf 2)$.
Holonomy $SU(2)$ is one factor, so $(\mathbf 1, \mathbf 2)$ consists of two singlets and $(\mathbf 2, \mathbf 1)$ of none:
two of the four spinor components survive, the fraction $\tfrac12$, and both have the same chirality.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the $SU(3)$ count of @exm-vcp-spinor-su3 by explicit gamma matrices. It also shows that
holonomy $U(3)$, a Kähler manifold that is not Ricci-flat, preserves nothing.

::: {#exr-vcp-spinor-count}
#### Invariant spinors with Sage

Build six $8 \times 8$ gamma matrices for $\mathbb{R}^6$, let $X \in \mathfrak{so}(6)$ act on spinors as $\tfrac14
X_{ab}\Gamma^a\Gamma^b$, find $\mathfrak{u}(3) = \{X : [X, J] = 0\}$ and its traceless part $\mathfrak{su}(3)$, and
compute the spinors annihilated by each.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The commutant of $J$ in $\mathfrak{so}(6)$ is $9$-dimensional and its subspace with $\operatorname{tr}(JX) = 0$ is
$8$-dimensional. The common kernel of $\mathfrak{su}(3)$ is $2$-dimensional, one spinor of each chirality, and that of
$\mathfrak{u}(3)$ is zero: the $U(1)$ factor rotates both singlets, which is why the Ricci-flat condition (vanishing
$U(1)$ part of the holonomy) is needed:

{{< sage exr-vcp-spinor-count >}}
:::

A parallel spinor constrains the curvature through its integrability condition. The second exercise derives the
Ricci-flatness stated in @prp-vcp-parallel-spinors. The argument uses only the Clifford algebra and the symmetries of the Riemann tensor.

::: {#exr-vcp-spinor-ricci}
#### Parallel spinors force Ricci-flatness

From $\nabla_m\xi = 0$ derive $R_{mnab}\Gamma^{ab}\xi = 0$, and using $\Gamma^n\Gamma^{ab}R_{mnab} = -2R_{ma}\Gamma^a$ (a
consequence of the first Bianchi identity) conclude that $R_{ma} = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The commutator of covariant derivatives on spinors is $[\nabla_m, \nabla_n]\xi = \tfrac14 R_{mnab}\Gamma^{ab}\xi$, which
vanishes for a parallel spinor. Multiplying by $\Gamma^n$ and summing, the totally antisymmetric part
$\Gamma^{nab}R_{mnab}$ drops out by the Bianchi identity $R_{m[nab]} = 0$ and what remains is $-2R_{ma}\Gamma^a\xi = 0$.
For a non-zero $\xi$ the vectors $\Gamma^a\xi$, $a = 1, \dots, n$, are linearly independent (multiply
$c_a\Gamma^a\xi = 0$ by $c_b\Gamma^b$ to get $|c|^2\xi = 0$), so $R_{ma} = 0$ for every $m$, $a$.
:::

Different higher-dimensional theories start with different numbers of supercharges. The third exercise turns the
fractions of @prp-vcp-parallel-spinors into four-dimensional $N$.

::: {#exr-vcp-spinor-fractions}
#### Four-dimensional supersymmetry

A four-dimensional supersymmetry has $4$ real supercharges. Find $N$ for: type IIA or IIB on a Calabi-Yau threefold
($32$ supercharges in ten dimensions); the heterotic string ($16$) on a Calabi-Yau threefold; M-theory ($32$) on a
$G_2$ manifold; type IIB on $K3 \times T^2$; M-theory on $T^7$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Type II on a Calabi-Yau threefold: $32/4 = 8$ supercharges, $N = 2$. Heterotic on a Calabi-Yau threefold: $16/4 = 4$,
$N = 1$, the phenomenologically preferred case. M-theory on $G_2$: $32/8 = 4$, $N = 1$. Type IIB on $K3 \times T^2$: the
holonomy $SU(2)$ keeps half, $16$ supercharges, $N = 4$. M-theory on $T^7$: all $32$, $N = 8$ (@def-supercharge-counting).
:::
::::

### Calabi-Yau threefolds

Holonomy $SU(3)$ in six dimensions is the case that preserves $N = 1$ for the heterotic string. Manifolds with this
holonomy are called Calabi-Yau, and Yau's theorem makes them easy to recognise from topology alone.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcp-calabi-yau}
#### Calabi-Yau manifold

A **Calabi-Yau manifold** of complex dimension $m$ is a compact, complex Kähler manifold whose holonomy is $SU(m)$
[@greene1997, Sec. 2.11]. Its metric is Ricci-flat, and it carries a nowhere-vanishing holomorphic $(m, 0)$-form $\Omega$,
parallel like the spinor of @prp-vcp-parallel-spinors. Conversely, by **Yau's theorem** a compact Kähler manifold with
vanishing first Chern class $c_1$ admits a unique Ricci-flat Kähler metric in each Kähler class [@greene1997, Sec. 2.11,
Theorem 2], so being Calabi-Yau is decided by the topological condition $c_1 = 0$. No Ricci-flat metric on a compact
Calabi-Yau threefold is known explicitly [@greene1997, Sec. 2.11].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}

:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
In complex dimension one the condition is satisfied by the torus. The holomorphic form is $dz$ and the holonomy is
trivial, which is $SU(1)$.

::: {#exm-vcp-cy-torus}
#### Elliptic curves

$T^2 = \mathbb{C}/\Lambda$ for a lattice $\Lambda$ is a compact Kähler manifold with flat metric and the nowhere-vanishing
holomorphic one-form $dz$: the one-dimensional Calabi-Yau manifolds are the elliptic curves. Its lattice, up to
rotation and scale, is the complex modulus $\tau$ of @sec-vi-flux.
:::

In complex dimension two there is, up to diffeomorphism, a single compact Calabi-Yau manifold with full $SU(2)$
holonomy, the K3 surface. Its simplest model is a quartic.

::: {#exm-vcp-cy-k3}
#### The K3 surface

The quartic $z_1^4 + z_2^4 + z_3^4 + z_4^4 = 0$ in $\mathbb{CP}^3$ has $c(TX) = (1 + J)^4/(1 + 4J) = 1 + 6J^2$, so
$c_1 = 0$, and Euler number $\int c_2 = 6\int J^2 = 24$ ($\int J^2 = 4$, the degree). It is the unique simply connected
two-dimensional Calabi-Yau [@greene1997, Sec. 2.11], with Hodge number $h^{1,1} = 20$ [@greene1997, eq. 2.76].
:::

The most studied threefold is the quintic. Its first Chern class vanishes because the degree equals the number of
homogeneous coordinates, the computation behind @prp-vcp-generations.

::: {#exm-vcp-cy-quintic}
#### The quintic

The quintic $X = \{z_1^5 + z_2^5 + z_3^5 + z_4^5 + z_5^5 = 0\} \subset \mathbb{CP}^4$ [@greene1997, eq. 2.65] has
$c(TX) = (1 + J)^5/(1 + 5J)$ by adjunction, with $J$ the hyperplane class [@greene1997, eq. 2.73]: $c_1 = (5 - 5)J = 0$,
so $X$ is a Calabi-Yau threefold. Changing the coefficients of the quintic polynomial changes the complex structure;
@def-vcp-hodge-number counts those changes.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise repeats the Chern class computation in every dimension. It finds the Calabi-Yau hypersurfaces of
projective spaces and their Euler numbers.

::: {#exr-vcp-cy-hypersurface}
#### Calabi-Yau hypersurfaces

For a hypersurface of degree $d$ in $\mathbb{CP}^{m+1}$, $c(TX) = (1 + J)^{m+2}/(1 + dJ)$ and $\int_X J^m = d$. Use Sage to
find, for $m = 1, \dots, 4$, the degrees with $c_1 = 0$ and the Euler numbers $\chi = \int c_m$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$c_1 = (m + 2 - d)J$, so $d = m + 2$: the cubic curve ($\chi = 0$, a torus), the quartic surface ($\chi = 24$, K3), the
quintic threefold ($\chi = -200$) and the sextic fourfold ($\chi = 2610$):

{{< sage exr-vcp-cy-hypersurface >}}
:::

Products of lower-dimensional Calabi-Yau manifolds are Ricci-flat and Kähler but have smaller holonomy. The second
exercise asks which products qualify under the definition.

::: {#exr-vcp-cy-products}
#### Products and tori

Are $T^6$, $T^2 \times K3$ and $K3 \times K3$ Calabi-Yau manifolds in the sense of @def-vcp-calabi-yau? What distinguishes
them from the quintic in terms of holomorphic one-forms?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
All three are compact, Kähler and Ricci-flat, but their holonomies, $\{1\}$, $SU(2)$ and $SU(2) \times SU(2)$, are proper
subgroups of $SU(m)$, so they are excluded by the definition (which asks for holonomy exactly $SU(m)$, as
@greene1997 [Sec. 2.8] does). $T^6$ and $T^2 \times K3$ have holomorphic one-forms ($dz$ on a torus factor), $h^{1,0} \ne
0$, while a Calabi-Yau threefold with full $SU(3)$ holonomy has $h^{1,0} = 0$ (@def-vcp-hodge-number). They preserve more
supersymmetry (@exr-vcp-holonomy-product) and are used for that reason in type II compactifications to $N = 4$.
:::

Yau's theorem trades a hard analytic problem, finding a Ricci-flat metric, for a topological one. The third exercise
explains why the first Chern class is the right obstruction.

::: {#exr-vcp-cy-ricci-form}
#### The Ricci form

On a Kähler manifold the Ricci tensor defines the closed $(1, 1)$-form $\rho = iR_{i\bar j}\,dz^i \wedge d\bar z^j$, which is
the curvature of the canonical line bundle and represents $2\pi c_1$. Explain why holonomy in $SU(m)$ implies $\rho = 0$,
and why $c_1 \ne 0$ rules out a Ricci-flat Kähler metric.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Levi-Civita connection of a Kähler metric takes values in $\mathfrak{u}(m) = \mathfrak{su}(m) \oplus \mathfrak{u}(1)$,
and the $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ part, the trace of the curvature, is the Ricci form [@greene1997, Sec. 2.11]. Holonomy in $SU(m)$
means the $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ part of the curvature vanishes, so $\rho = 0$. Conversely, if a Ricci-flat Kähler metric
existed then $\rho = 0$ would represent $2\pi c_1$, so $c_1 = 0$ in real cohomology: a manifold with $c_1 \ne 0$, such as
$\mathbb{CP}^m$ with $c_1 = (m + 1)J$, has no Ricci-flat Kähler metric.
:::
::::

The topology of a Calabi-Yau threefold is summarised by its Hodge numbers. Two of them are free and the rest are fixed
by the holonomy; the free ones count both the moduli and the generations.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcp-hodge-number}
#### Hodge number

On a compact Kähler manifold the **Hodge number** $h^{p,q}$ is the dimension of the space of harmonic $(p, q)$-forms,
equivalently of the Dolbeault cohomology $H^{p,q}_{\bar\partial}(X)$. They satisfy $h^{p,q} = h^{q,p} = h^{m-p,m-q}$ and
$b_k = \sum_{p+q=k}h^{p,q}$ [@greene1997, eqs. 2.55-2.57], and the Euler number is $\chi = \sum_{p,q}(-1)^{p+q}h^{p,q}$
[@greene1997, eq. 2.75]. On a Calabi-Yau threefold $h^{0,0} = h^{3,0} = 1$ and $h^{1,0} = h^{2,0} = 0$
[@greene1997, Sec. 2.11], so the **Hodge diamond** depends on $h^{1,1}$ and $h^{2,1}$ only and
$$
\chi = 2\left(h^{1,1} - h^{2,1}\right) .
$$ {#eq-vcp-euler-hodge}
Ricci-flat deformations of the metric are counted by $h^{1,1}$ (real Kähler moduli) and $h^{2,1}$ (complex
complex-structure moduli) [@greene1997, Sec. 2.12].
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![Hodge diamonds of two Calabi-Yau threefolds: the quintic in $\mathbb{CP}^4$ ($h^{1,1} = 1$, $h^{2,1} = 101$, $\chi = -
200$) and the resolved orbifold $T^6/\mathbb{Z}_3$ ($h^{1,1} = 36$, $h^{2,1} = 0$, $\chi = 72$). Row $k$ from the top
lists $h^{p,q}$ with $p + q = k$; the free entries are coloured. Generated by
`figures/hodge_diamond.sage`.](figures/hodge_diamond.svg){#fig-hodge-diamond width=85%}

The quintic is the standard example. Its Hodge numbers follow from the Euler number and from counting the
coefficients of the defining polynomial, as @prp-vcp-generations checks.

::: {#exm-vcp-hodge-quintic}
#### The quintic

The quintic has $h^{1,1} = 1$ (the hyperplane class, inherited from $\mathbb{CP}^4$) and $h^{2,1} = 101$, so $\chi = 2(1 -
101) = -200$ [@greene1997, Sec. 2.12], in agreement with the Chern class computation of @exm-vcp-cy-quintic
(@fig-hodge-diamond). Its third Betti number is $b_3 = 2 + 2h^{2,1} = 204$.
:::

Calabi-Yau threefolds come in mirror pairs whose Hodge diamonds are reflections of each other. The two kinds of moduli
are exchanged, and with them the sign of the Euler number.

::: {#exm-vcp-hodge-mirror}
#### Mirror symmetry

The mirror quintic has $(h^{1,1}, h^{2,1}) = (101, 1)$ and $\chi = +200$ [@greene1997, Table 1]. In general mirror pairs
satisfy $h^{1,1}(M) = h^{2,1}(\tilde M)$ and $h^{2,1}(M) = h^{1,1}(\tilde M)$ [@greene1997, eq. 6.2] and define the same
string theory, with Kähler and complex-structure deformations exchanged.
:::

The Hodge numbers count the massless scalars of a compactification. For the quintic the numbers are already large,
which is the moduli problem of @sec-vi-flux.

::: {#exm-vcp-hodge-moduli}
#### Moduli of the quintic

The quintic has $1$ Kähler modulus (its overall size) and $101$ complex-structure moduli, a moduli space of real dimension
$2 \cdot 101 + 1 = 203$ [@greene1997, Sec. 2.12]. In a type II compactification each becomes a massless
four-dimensional scalar, together with partners from the other higher-dimensional fields; none has a potential until
fluxes are switched on (@def-vcp-flux-potential).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Betti numbers follow from the diamond by summing rows. The first exercise does this for three threefolds and checks
Poincaré duality.

::: {#exr-vcp-hodge-betti}
#### Betti numbers from the diamond

Compute $b_0, \dots, b_6$ for the quintic, the mirror quintic and the resolved $T^6/\mathbb{Z}_3$ from their Hodge numbers
with Sage, and check $b_k = b_{6-k}$ and $\sum(-1)^kb_k = 2(h^{1,1} - h^{2,1})$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The quintic has $(b_0, \dots, b_6) = (1, 0, 1, 204, 1, 0, 1)$, the mirror $(1, 0, 101, 4, 101, 0, 1)$ and $T^6/\mathbb{Z}_3$
$(1, 0, 36, 2, 36, 0, 1)$; all are palindromic and their alternating sums are $-200$, $200$ and $72$:

{{< sage exr-vcp-hodge-betti >}}
:::

The number $h^{2,1} = 101$ of the quintic can be found without any cohomology. The second exercise counts the
deformations of the defining polynomial.

::: {#exr-vcp-hodge-monomials}
#### Counting deformations

The quintics form a projective space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $5$ in five variables, and two of them related
by a linear change of coordinates define the same manifold. Count the monomials with Sage and subtract $\dim GL(5)$ to
recover $h^{2,1} = 101$ [@greene1997, Sec. 2.12]; do the same for the quartic K3 surface.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
There are $\binom{9}{4} = 126$ quintic monomials and $\dim GL(5) = 25$, leaving $101$ parameters, the complex-structure
moduli. For quartics in $\mathbb{CP}^3$, $\binom{7}{3} = 35$ monomials minus $16$ leave $19$, the algebraic deformations of
K3 (its $h^{1,1} = 20$ includes the polarisation class):

{{< sage exr-vcp-hodge-monomials >}}
:::

The formula @eq-vcp-euler-hodge uses all the symmetries of the diamond at once. The third exercise derives it by hand. Only the symmetries of the diamond are needed.

::: {#exr-vcp-hodge-euler}
#### The Euler number of a threefold

Write out $\chi = \sum(-1)^{p+q}h^{p,q}$ for a Calabi-Yau threefold using $h^{p,q} = h^{q,p} = h^{3-p,3-q}$ and the values
fixed by the holonomy, and derive @eq-vcp-euler-hodge.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The even rows contribute $h^{0,0} + (h^{2,0} + h^{1,1} + h^{0,2}) + (h^{3,1} + h^{2,2} + h^{1,3}) + h^{3,3} = 1 + h^{1,1} +
h^{1,1} + 1$, using $h^{2,0} = h^{3,1} = 0$ and $h^{2,2} = h^{1,1}$. The odd rows contribute $-(h^{1,0} + h^{0,1}) - (h^{3,0} +
h^{2,1} + h^{1,2} + h^{0,3}) - (h^{3,2} + h^{2,3}) = -(2 + 2h^{2,1})$. The sum is $2h^{1,1} - 2h^{2,1}$.
:::
::::

### $G_2$ manifolds

In seven dimensions the group that fixes a spinor is the exceptional group $G_2$. It is defined by a three-form, and
manifolds with this holonomy are the internal spaces of M-theory with four-dimensional $N = 1$ supersymmetry.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcp-g2-manifold}
#### $G_2$ manifold

On $\mathbb{R}^7$ with coordinates $x_1, \dots, x_7$ let $\Phi = \sum dx_i \wedge dx_j \wedge dx_k$, summed over the seven
triples $(ijk) = (123), (147), (165), (246), (257), (354), (367)$; its stabiliser in $GL(7, \mathbb{R})$ is the
fourteen-dimensional group $G_2$, the automorphism group of the octonions [@acharya2004, eqs. 2.6-2.8]. A **$G_2$
manifold** is a seven-manifold with a three-form $\Phi$ that has this form at every point in a suitable frame and satisfies
$$
d\Phi = 0, \qquad d{*\Phi} = 0 ;
$$ {#eq-vcp-g2-torsion-free}
then $\Phi$ determines a metric whose holonomy lies in $G_2$ [@acharya2004, eqs. 2.14, 2.17]. The metric is Ricci-flat
and has a parallel spinor.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The flat model is the definition itself. The dimension count shows why a generic three-form in seven dimensions has
the $G_2$ form.

::: {#exm-vcp-g2-flat}
#### The flat model

On $\mathbb{R}^7$ the constant form $\Phi$ is closed and coclosed, with holonomy trivial. Its orbit under $GL(7)$ has
dimension $49 - 14 = 35 = \dim\Lambda^3\mathbb{R}^7$, so the orbit is open: a generic three-form is of $G_2$ type
(@exr-vcp-g2-stabiliser), which is why a $G_2$ structure is defined by a single form.
:::

A Calabi-Yau threefold times a circle is a $G_2$ manifold with smaller holonomy. The three-form is built from the
Kähler form and the holomorphic three-form.

::: {#exm-vcp-g2-cy}
#### Calabi-Yau times a circle

On $CY_3 \times S^1$ with Kähler form $J$ and holomorphic three-form $\Omega$, the form $\Phi = J \wedge d\theta +
\operatorname{Re}\Omega$ satisfies @eq-vcp-g2-torsion-free because $dJ = 0$ and $d\Omega = 0$. The holonomy is $SU(3)
\subset G_2$, two parallel spinors survive, and M-theory on it is type IIA on the Calabi-Yau with $N = 2$
(@exr-vcp-g2-spinors).
:::

Compact manifolds with full $G_2$ holonomy are hard to construct. The first examples were resolved orbifolds of the
seven-torus, and their Betti numbers fix the spectrum.

::: {#exm-vcp-g2-joyce}
#### Joyce's orbifold

Joyce resolved the orbifold $T^7/\mathbb{Z}_2^3$, with three commuting involutions acting by sign changes and half
shifts of the coordinates, to a compact $G_2$ manifold with $b_2 = 12$ and $b_3 = 43$ [@acharya2004, eqs. 3.22-3.24].
M-theory on a smooth $G_2$ manifold gives four-dimensional $N = 1$ supergravity with $b_2$ abelian vector multiplets and
$b_3$ neutral chiral multiplets [@acharya2004, Sec. 4]: here $12$ and $43$.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes the dimension of $G_2$ from its definition. It solves the linear conditions for an
infinitesimal transformation to preserve $\Phi$.

::: {#exr-vcp-g2-stabiliser}
#### The Lie algebra of $G_2$ with Sage

A matrix $X \in \mathfrak{gl}(7)$ acts on three-forms by $(X\cdot\Phi)_{ijk} = X^l{}_i\Phi_{ljk} + X^l{}_j\Phi_{ilk} +
X^l{}_k\Phi_{ijl}$. Solve $X\cdot\Phi = 0$ with Sage, find its dimension, and show that its solutions are antisymmetric.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The $35$ conditions have rank $35$, so the stabiliser has dimension $49 - 35 = 14$, and every solution is antisymmetric:
$\mathfrak g_2 \subset \mathfrak{so}(7)$, so $\Phi$ also fixes a metric:

{{< sage exr-vcp-g2-stabiliser >}}
:::

The spectrum of M-theory on a smooth $G_2$ manifold contains only abelian vectors and neutral scalars. The second
exercise counts the fields of Joyce's example and asks where non-abelian gauge groups could come from.

::: {#exr-vcp-g2-spectrum}
#### The spectrum of a smooth $G_2$ compactification

For $b_2 = 12$, $b_3 = 43$, count the real scalars and the vectors of the four-dimensional theory, explaining which come
from the metric and which from the three-form potential $C$ of eleven-dimensional supergravity. Why is there no
non-abelian gauge symmetry, unlike in Part IV?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$C = \sum\phi_I\omega^I$ with $\omega^I$ the harmonic three-forms gives $b_3 = 43$ real scalars, and the deformations of
$\Phi$ (equivalently of the metric) another $43$; they pair into $43$ complex scalars $\int_{\alpha_I}(\Phi + iC)$, the
chiral multiplets. $C = \sum A_\alpha\wedge\beta^\alpha$ with $\beta^\alpha$ the harmonic two-forms gives $b_2 = 12$ abelian
vectors [@acharya2004, Sec. 4]. A compact manifold with full $G_2$ holonomy has $b_1 = 0$ and no continuous isometries, so
no Kaluza-Klein gauge fields arise; non-abelian gauge groups and charged chiral matter come only from singularities of
the $G_2$ manifold [@acharya2004, Sec. 4].
:::

The amount of supersymmetry preserved on $CY_3 \times S^1$ follows from branching the spinor through the chain
$SU(3) \subset G_2 \subset Spin(7)$. The third exercise performs the branching.

::: {#exr-vcp-g2-spinors}
#### Spinors on $CY_3 \times S^1$

Under $SU(3) \subset G_2$ the vector of $G_2$ decomposes as $\mathbf 7 = \mathbf 3 + \bar{\mathbf 3} + \mathbf 1$. Use
$\mathbf 8 = \mathbf 7 + \mathbf 1$ to count the spinors of $Spin(7)$ invariant under $SU(3)$, and deduce the
four-dimensional $N$ of M-theory on $CY_3 \times S^1$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\mathbf 8 = \mathbf 7 + \mathbf 1 = \mathbf 3 + \bar{\mathbf 3} + \mathbf 1 + \mathbf 1$: two singlets, the fraction
$\tfrac14$, so $32/4 = 8$ supercharges and $N = 2$, the same as type IIA on the Calabi-Yau threefold, which is what M-theory
on a circle becomes.
:::
::::

### Nearly-Kähler coset spaces

Relaxing parallel to almost parallel gives manifolds with a $G$-structure and torsion. In six dimensions the most
symmetric of them are coset spaces, which is where CSDR and supersymmetric compactifications meet.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcp-nearly-kahler}
#### Nearly-Kähler manifold

A six-manifold with an $SU(3)$-structure, a real two-form $J$ and a complex three-form $\Omega$ obtained from a
nowhere-vanishing spinor, has $dJ$ and $d\Omega$ decomposed into five **torsion classes** $\mathcal W_1, \dots,
\mathcal W_5$ [@chatzistavrakidis2009nk, eq. 2.4]:
$$
dJ = \tfrac32 i\left(\mathcal W_1\Omega^* - \mathcal W_1^*\Omega\right) + \mathcal W_4 \wedge J + \mathcal W_3, \qquad
d\Omega = \mathcal W_1 J \wedge J + \mathcal W_2 \wedge J + \mathcal W_5^* \wedge \Omega .
$$ {#eq-vcp-torsion-classes}
A Calabi-Yau manifold has all five zero. A **nearly-Kähler manifold** has only $\mathcal W_1 \ne 0$: it is neither
Kähler nor complex [@chatzistavrakidis2009nk, Sec. 2.2.2]. The homogeneous nearly-Kähler six-manifolds are the three
non-symmetric coset spaces of equal rank, $G_2/SU(3)$, $Sp(4)/(SU(2) \times U(1))$ and $SU(3)/(U(1) \times U(1))$, and the
group manifold $SU(2) \times SU(2)$ [@chatzistavrakidis2009nk, Sec. 2.2.2].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The six-sphere is the simplest example. It is a coset of the exceptional group, and its nearly-Kähler structure comes
from the octonions.

::: {#exm-vcp-nk-sphere}
#### $G_2/SU(3) = S^6$

$G_2/SU(3)$ is the six-sphere with a $G_2$-invariant almost complex structure. With radius $R_1$, $J = R_1^2\omega_1$ and
$\Omega = R_1^3(\rho_2 + i\rho_1)$ for the invariant forms $\omega_1$, $\rho_{1,2}$, and $\mathcal W_1 = -2i/(\sqrt3R_1)$ is the
only torsion class [@chatzistavrakidis2009nk, eqs. B.5-B.9]: nearly-Kähler for every radius.
:::

With more than one invariant two-form the coset has several radii, and only a special ratio is nearly-Kähler. The flag
manifold is the important case.

::: {#exm-vcp-nk-flag}
#### $SU(3)/(U(1) \times U(1))$

The flag manifold has three invariant two-forms and three radii $R_1, R_2, R_3$, with $J = \sum_iR_i^2\omega_i$ and
$\Omega = R_1R_2R_3(\rho_2 + i\rho_1)$; the class $\mathcal W_2$ is non-zero unless $R_1 = R_2 = R_3$
[@chatzistavrakidis2009nk, eqs. 2.5-2.6, B.30-B.31], and only at equal radii is the coset nearly-Kähler, and then Einstein
(@exr-vcp-nk-torsion).
:::

These cosets are the internal spaces of CSDR models with realistic gauge groups. The flag manifold gives three
generations, as the counting of @prp-vcp-generations shows.

::: {#exm-vcp-nk-csdr}
#### CSDR over the flag manifold

Reducing ten-dimensional $E_8$ super-Yang-Mills over $SU(3)/(U(1) \times U(1))$ with the CSDR rules of
@sec-csdr-symmetric-fields gives a four-dimensional $E_6$ gauge theory (with two global $U(1)$s) and three chiral
multiplets in the $\mathbf{27}$: an $N = 1$ $E_6$ grand unified theory with three families, softly broken by terms the
geometry supplies [@manolakos2016, Sec. 2; @chatzistavrakidis2009nk, Sec. 4.3]. Over $G_2/SU(3)$ the same gives one family
and over $Sp(4)/(SU(2) \times U(1))$ two [@chatzistavrakidis2009nk, Secs. 4.1-4.2].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The torsion classes of the flag manifold depend on the three radii through explicit polynomials. The first exercise
finds where $\mathcal W_2$ vanishes.

::: {#exr-vcp-nk-torsion}
#### The nearly-Kähler point with Sage

The class $\mathcal W_2$ of $SU(3)/(U(1) \times U(1))$ has the three coefficients $R_i^2(2R_i^2 - R_j^2 - R_k^2)$, and
$\mathcal W_1 = -\tfrac{2i}{3}(R_1^2 + R_2^2 + R_3^2)/(R_1R_2R_3)$ [@chatzistavrakidis2009nk, eqs. B.30-B.31]. Solve
$\mathcal W_2 = 0$ for positive radii with Sage, evaluate $\mathcal W_1$ there, and repeat for $Sp(4)/(SU(2) \times U(1))$,
whose $\mathcal W_2$ has coefficients proportional to $R_1^2 - R_2^2$ [@chatzistavrakidis2009nk, eq. B.20].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The only positive solution is $R_1 = R_2 = R_3 = R$, where $\mathcal W_1 = -2i/R$; for $Sp(4)/(SU(2) \times U(1))$ it is $R_1
= R_2 = R$, with the same $\mathcal W_1 = -2i/R$. At any other radii the coset has an $SU(3)$-structure that is not
nearly-Kähler:

{{< sage exr-vcp-nk-torsion >}}
:::

The rank condition in @def-vcp-nearly-kahler is not decoration. The second exercise relates it to chirality and to the
Euler number.

::: {#exr-vcp-nk-rank}
#### Why equal rank

The Euler number of a compact coset $G/H$ is $|W_G|/|W_H|$ when $\operatorname{rank}G = \operatorname{rank}H$ and $0$
otherwise. Use this to explain why the group manifold $SU(2) \times SU(2)$, although nearly-Kähler, gives no chiral
generations, while the three equal-rank cosets do.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The number of net generations is half the Euler number of the internal space [@chatzistavrakidis2009nk, Sec. 4.1]. A
group manifold has a nowhere-vanishing left-invariant vector field, so its Euler number is zero and it gives no net
chirality; the authors exclude it for this reason [@chatzistavrakidis2009nk, Sec. 6]. The equal-rank cosets have $\chi =
12/6 = 2$, $8/2 = 4$ and $6/1 = 6$ (@prp-vcp-generations), hence one, two and three generations.
:::

A nearly-Kähler manifold is Einstein with positive curvature, so it cannot be the internal space of a vacuum with flat
spacetime and nothing else switched on. The third exercise quantifies this for the six-sphere.

::: {#exr-vcp-nk-einstein}
#### Positive curvature

The round $S^6$ of radius $R$ has $R_{mn} = \tfrac{5}{R^2}\gamma_{mn}$. Explain why $\mathbb{R}^4 \times S^6$ is not a solution
of the ten-dimensional vacuum Einstein equations, and what the dimensional reduction produces instead.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The vacuum equations ask for $R_{MN} = 0$, while the sphere has $R_{mn} \ne 0$: the internal curvature acts as a source.
After reduction it appears as a negative contribution to the four-dimensional potential, proportional to the internal
scalar curvature with a minus sign (@def-cosmological-constant); for $G_2/SU(3)$ the reduced gravitational potential is
$V_{\rm grav} = -15e^{-\tilde\phi}/(\kappa^2R_1^2)$ [@chatzistavrakidis2009nk, eq. 4.2], which must be balanced by
fluxes or condensates, or accepted as an anti-de Sitter vacuum. This is the same competition as in the flux potential of
@def-vcp-flux-potential.
:::
::::

### Orbifolds

A torus has trivial holonomy, but its quotient by a finite group of rotations has holonomy that finite group, at least
away from the fixed points. Toroidal orbifolds are therefore the simplest compact spaces with reduced holonomy, and the
only ones on which everything can be computed.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcp-toroidal-orbifold}
#### Toroidal orbifold

Let $\Lambda \subset \mathbb{C}^m$ be a lattice and $\Gamma$ a finite group of unitary maps of $\mathbb{C}^m$ preserving
$\Lambda$. The **toroidal orbifold** $T^{2m}/\Gamma$ is the quotient of the torus $\mathbb{C}^m/\Lambda$ by the induced
action of $\Gamma$. Points fixed by a non-trivial element are conical singularities; away from them the quotient is a
flat manifold with holonomy $\Gamma$. If $\Gamma \subset SU(m)$ the holomorphic $m$-form $dz^1 \wedge \dots \wedge dz^m$ is
invariant and the singularities can be resolved to a Calabi-Yau manifold. The standard example is $T^6/\mathbb{Z}_3$: the
hexagonal lattice $\mathbb{Z} + \mathbb{Z}\omega$, $\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}$, in each of three complex planes, with $\mathbb{Z}_3$
acting by $z^i \mapsto \omega z^i$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![The orbifold $T^2/\mathbb{Z}_3$. The hexagonal lattice $\mathbb{Z} + \mathbb{Z}\omega$ (dots; red the corners of a cell), a
cell of the torus (dashed) made of two equilateral triangles, and a fundamental domain of $z \mapsto \omega z$ (blue), one
third of the cell. The three fixed points modulo the lattice are $0$ (red) and the centres $(2 + \omega)/3$ (green) and
$(1 + 2\omega)/3$ (orange) of the triangles; gluing the edges of the blue rhombus gives a sphere with three cone points of
angle $2\pi/3$. Generated by `figures/z3_orbifold.sage`.](figures/z3_orbifold.svg){#fig-z3-orbifold width=60%}

{{< interactive z3_orbifold 460 >}}

The circle with a reflection is the simplest orbifold, an interval with two fixed endpoints. It is the fifth dimension
of the Randall-Sundrum model.

::: {#exm-vcp-orbifold-interval}
#### $S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$

The circle of radius $r_c$ with $y \mapsto -y$ has the fixed points $y = 0$ and $y = \pi r_c$, and the quotient is the
interval $[0, \pi r_c]$. Fields are even or odd under the reflection, and the odd ones vanish at the fixed points. The
two fixed points are where the branes of @def-vcp-rs-metric sit [@randall1999a, Sec. 2].
:::

On the hexagonal torus the rotation by $120°$ fixes three points. The quotient is a sphere with three cone points
(@fig-z3-orbifold).

::: {#exm-vcp-orbifold-t2z3}
#### $T^2/\mathbb{Z}_3$

In lattice coordinates $z = x + y\omega$ the rotation is $M = \begin{pmatrix}0 & -1\\ 1 & -1\end{pmatrix}$, and $z$ is
fixed modulo $\Lambda$ when $(M - 1)(x, y)^T \in \mathbb{Z}^2$: the three points $0$, $(2 + \omega)/3$, $(1 + 2\omega)/3$,
as many as $\det(1 - M) = 3$ (@prp-vcp-generations). The fundamental domain has a third of the area of the cell.
:::

Taking three copies gives the six-dimensional orbifold. The holomorphic three-form is invariant because $\omega^3 = 1$,
so the group lies in $SU(3)$.

::: {#exm-vcp-orbifold-t6z3}
#### $T^6/\mathbb{Z}_3$

On $T^6 = (T^2)^3$ with $z^i \mapsto \omega z^i$ there are $3^3 = 27$ fixed points, and $dz^1 \wedge dz^2 \wedge dz^3 \mapsto
\omega^3\,dz^1 \wedge dz^2 \wedge dz^3$ is invariant: $\mathbb{Z}_3 \subset SU(3)$ and one quarter of the supersymmetry
survives. The invariant forms $dz^i \wedge d\bar z^j$ give $h^{1,1} = 9$, no $(2, 1)$-form is invariant, and each fixed point
contributes one more $(1, 1)$-class: $h^{1,1} = 36$, $h^{2,1} = 0$ (@fig-hodge-diamond).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
Other lattices allow other rotations. The first exercise finds the fixed points of the $\mathbb{Z}_4$ rotation of the
square torus.

::: {#exr-vcp-orbifold-z4}
#### $T^2/\mathbb{Z}_4$ with Sage

On $\mathbb{C}/(\mathbb{Z} + i\mathbb{Z})$ find with Sage the points fixed by $z \mapsto iz$, by $z \mapsto -z$ and by $z
\mapsto -iz$ modulo the lattice, compare their numbers with $\det(1 - M^k)$, and identify the cone points of the
quotient.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$z \mapsto \pm iz$ fixes $0$ and $(1 + i)/2$ ($\det(1 - M) = 2$); $z \mapsto -z$ fixes the four half-periods ($\det(1 - M^2) =
4$), of which $1/2$ and $i/2$ are exchanged by $z \mapsto iz$. The quotient has cone points of angles $2\pi/4$, $2\pi/4$
(from $0$ and $(1 + i)/2$) and $2\pi/2$ (the orbit $\{1/2, i/2\}$), and the Riemann-Hurwitz count $0/4 + \tfrac34 + \tfrac34 +
\tfrac12 = 2$ shows that it is a sphere:

{{< sage exr-vcp-orbifold-z4 >}}
:::

Orbifolds can act on the internal indices of fields as well as on space. The second exercise follows the
$\mathbb{Z}_3$ projection of a gauge theory, which produces three chiral generations in the same way as $T^6/\mathbb{Z}_3$.

::: {#exr-vcp-orbifold-gauge}
#### The $\mathbb{Z}_3$ projection of a gauge theory

Take $N = 4$ super-Yang-Mills with gauge group $SU(3N)$ and let $\mathbb{Z}_3$ act on the three adjoint chiral multiplets
$\Phi^i$ by $\omega$ (embedded in $SU(3)$ of the $R$-symmetry) and on gauge indices by $\gamma_3 = \operatorname{diag}(1_N,
\omega1_N, \omega^21_N)$. Find the surviving gauge group and chiral multiplets.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Gauge fields must commute with $\gamma_3$, leaving $SU(N)^3$. A component $\Phi^i_{IJ}$ between blocks $I$ and $J$ picks up
$\omega^{I - J + 1}$ and survives when $J = I + 1 \bmod 3$: for each $i$ the bifundamentals $(N, \bar N, 1) + (1, N, \bar N) +
(\bar N, 1, N)$, three copies in all. They are chiral (no conjugates appear), anomaly free, and the three copies are three
generations [@chatzistavrakidis2010orb, Sec. 2].
:::

The quotient of a surface by a finite group has an Euler number computable from the fixed points. The third exercise
identifies $T^2/\mathbb{Z}_3$ topologically.

::: {#exr-vcp-orbifold-sphere}
#### The topology of $T^2/\mathbb{Z}_3$

Use the Riemann-Hurwitz formula $\chi(T^2) = |\Gamma|\left(\chi(Q) - \sum_i(1 - 1/m_i)\right)$, where $Q$ is the quotient
and $m_i$ the orders of the stabilisers of the cone points, to identify $T^2/\mathbb{Z}_3$. Check it against the gluing of
the rhombus in @fig-z3-orbifold.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$0 = 3(\chi(Q) - 3 \cdot \tfrac23)$ gives $\chi(Q) = 2$: a sphere. Gluing the rhombus, the two edges at the vertex $0$ are
identified by the rotation through $120°$ about $0$, and the two edges at each centre by the rotation about that centre,
so each of the three points becomes a cone point of angle $2\pi/3$ and the result is a sphere, a "triangular pillow".
:::
::::

Every count of this section reduces to arithmetic with Chern classes, Hodge numbers, Weyl groups and fixed points. The
proposition collects the computations, which are checked exactly in Sage.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-vcp-generations}
#### Euler numbers and generations

(a) A degree-$t$ hypersurface in $\mathbb{CP}^4$ has $c_1 = (5 - t)J$; for the quintic $c(TX) = 1 + 10J^2 - 40J^3$, so
$\chi = -40\int J^3 = -200$, and $h^{2,1} = \binom94 - 25 = 101$, $h^{1,1} = 1$, $\chi = 2(h^{1,1} - h^{2,1})$.
(b) The resolved $T^6/\mathbb{Z}_3$ has $27$ fixed points ($\det(1 - M) = 3$ in each plane), $h^{1,1} = 9 + 27 = 36$,
$h^{2,1} = 0$ and orbifold Euler number $\tfrac13 \cdot 8 \cdot 27 = 72 = 2(36 - 0)$.
(c) The nearly-Kähler cosets have $\chi = |W_G|/|W_H|$: $\chi(G_2/SU(3)) = 2$, $\chi(Sp(4)/(SU(2) \times U(1))) = 4$,
$\chi(SU(3)/(U(1) \times U(1))) = 6$.
With the rule that the net number of chiral generations is $|\chi|/2$ [@chatzistavrakidis2009nk, Sec. 4.1], which for a
Calabi-Yau threefold in the heterotic string with the spin connection embedded in the gauge group reads $|h^{1,1} -
h^{2,1}|$ (quoted, not derived), the quintic gives $100$ generations, $T^6/\mathbb{Z}_3$ gives $36$ and the three cosets
give $1$, $2$, $3$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Checked by exact computation in `figures/hodge_diamond.sage` and `figures/z3_orbifold.sage`: the Chern classes as
power series, the monomial count, the alternating sums of the diamonds, the Weyl group orders, and the fixed points by
exhaustive search over $\tfrac13\Lambda$. The generation rule is quoted, not derived.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The quintic gives far too many generations. Dividing by a freely acting group divides the Euler number, which is how
models with few generations were first built.

::: {#exm-vcp-generations-quotient}
#### Free quotients

If a finite group $G$ acts freely on $X$, then $\chi(X/G) = \chi(X)/|G|$. Special quintics admit a free action of
$\mathbb{Z}_5 \times \mathbb{Z}_5$, giving $\chi = -200/25 = -8$ and $4$ net generations (@exr-vcp-generations-chern).
Three generations need $|\chi| = 6$, which requires other constructions.
:::

The orbifold has positive Euler number and no complex-structure moduli. Its $36$ generations are counted with the
opposite chirality to those of the quintic.

::: {#exm-vcp-generations-orbifold}
#### $T^6/\mathbb{Z}_3$

With $h^{1,1} = 36$ and $h^{2,1} = 0$ the resolved orbifold has $\chi = 72$ and $36$ net generations
(@fig-hodge-diamond), the sign of $\chi$ distinguishing the $\mathbf{27}$ from the $\overline{\mathbf{27}}$ of $E_6$. Its
$27$ fixed points carry the twisted-sector states: in the string they are where most of the charged matter sits.
:::

For the cosets the counting is in agreement with the explicit CSDR spectra. Each $\mathbf{27}$ of $E_6$ that survives the
reduction is one generation.

::: {#exm-vcp-generations-cosets}
#### The CSDR spectra

The CSDR reductions of @exm-vcp-nk-csdr give one, two and three chiral multiplets in the $\mathbf{27}$ of $E_6$ over
$G_2/SU(3)$, $Sp(4)/(SU(2) \times U(1))$ and $SU(3)/(U(1) \times U(1))$, matching $\chi/2 = 1, 2, 3$
[@chatzistavrakidis2009nk, Secs. 4.1-4.3]. The flag manifold is the only homogeneous nearly-Kähler space with three
families.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise checks the Chern classes of the quintic to third order and the effect of free quotients. It uses
Sage's power series.

::: {#exr-vcp-generations-chern}
#### Chern classes with Sage

Expand $(1 + J)^5/(1 + 5J)$ with Sage, compute $\int c_2 \wedge J$ and $\int c_3$ using $\int J^3 = 5$, and tabulate the
Euler number and the number of generations of free quotients by groups of order $5$ and $25$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$c(TX) = 1 + 10J^2 - 40J^3$, $\int c_2J = 50$, $\int c_3 = -200$; free quotients of order $5$ and $25$ have $\chi = -40$ and
$-8$, that is $20$ and $4$ generations:

{{< sage exr-vcp-generations-chern >}}
:::

The Weyl group formula for the Euler number applies to every equal-rank coset. The second exercise checks it on spaces
whose Euler numbers are known independently.

::: {#exr-vcp-generations-weyl}
#### Euler numbers of cosets with Sage

Compute $|W_G|/|W_H|$ with Sage for $SU(2)/U(1)$, $SU(3)/U(2)$ and the three nearly-Kähler cosets, and compare with
$\chi(S^2) = 2$, $\chi(\mathbb{CP}^2) = 3$ and $\chi(S^6) = 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$2/1 = 2$, $6/2 = 3$, $12/6 = 2$, $8/2 = 4$ and $6/1 = 6$, in agreement with the known values; half of the last three
are the generation numbers:

{{< sage exr-vcp-generations-weyl >}}
:::

The orbifold Euler number is not the Euler number of the singular quotient space. The third exercise compares the two
and explains why the orbifold formula is the physically relevant one.

::: {#exr-vcp-generations-orbifold-euler}
#### Two Euler numbers of $T^6/\mathbb{Z}_3$

The topological Euler number of the quotient space is $\chi(T^6/\mathbb{Z}_3) = \tfrac13(\chi(T^6) - 27) + 27$. Compute it,
compare with the orbifold Euler number $72$, and explain the difference in terms of the resolution of the $27$
singularities.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\tfrac13(0 - 27) + 27 = 18$. Resolving each singularity $\mathbb{C}^3/\mathbb{Z}_3$ replaces a point by a copy of
$\mathbb{CP}^2$, with Euler number $3$, so the resolved manifold has $\chi = 18 - 27 + 27 \cdot 3 = 72$, the orbifold Euler
number: the string computes on the orbifold the topology of its smooth resolution, the twisted sectors supplying the
$27$ extra classes.
:::
::::

## Flux compactifications {#sec-vi-flux}

A Calabi-Yau compactification solves the vacuum equations for every value of its Kähler and complex-structure
parameters, so each parameter becomes a massless scalar in four dimensions, hundreds of them for the quintic. Such
scalars would mediate long-range forces and let the constants of nature drift. Fluxes, quantised field strengths
threading the cycles of the internal space, cost an energy that depends on the shape and size of the cycles and so
give the moduli a potential. This section defines moduli and fluxes, proves the Dirac quantisation that makes fluxes
integers, finds the minimum of the flux potential in a one-modulus model, and sketches the landscape of vacua that the
many integer choices produce.

### Moduli

The vacuum equations of higher-dimensional gravity rarely fix the internal geometry completely. A family of solutions
labelled by continuous parameters gives, after reduction, scalars whose expectation values can be anything.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcp-modulus}
#### Modulus

A **modulus** of a compactification is a parameter of a continuous family of vacuum solutions $M_4 \times X_t$, $t \in
\mathcal M$; the parameter space $\mathcal M$ is the **moduli space**. Promoting $t$ to a function of the
four-dimensional coordinates gives a massless scalar with no potential, a flat direction of the reduced theory. Ricci-flat
metrics always come in families with at least one parameter, their overall scale, and moduli exist without any symmetry
behind them, unlike Goldstone bosons [@douglas2006, Sec. II.B]. Massless moduli coupled with gravitational strength are
excluded by tests of Newton's law, which bound their masses from below by about $10^{-3}$ eV [@douglas2006, Sec. I].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The radius of the Kaluza-Klein circle is the first modulus. Nothing in the five-dimensional vacuum equations prefers
one radius over another.

::: {#exm-vcp-modulus-circle}
#### The Kaluza-Klein radius

$M_4 \times S^1_R$ is a solution of the five-dimensional vacuum Einstein equations for every $R$, because the Einstein
equations are invariant under constant rescalings of the metric. The scalar $\phi$ of @def-kk-ansatz is the modulus
$R$ promoted to a field, massless and coupled to all matter [@douglas2006, Sec. I].
:::

A flat torus has as many moduli as there are constant metrics on it. In two dimensions they are the area and the
complex structure of the torus.

::: {#exm-vcp-modulus-torus}
#### Moduli of a torus

Every constant positive-definite metric $g_{mn}$ on $T^n = \mathbb{R}^n/\mathbb{Z}^n$ is flat, which gives $n(n + 1)/2$
moduli. For $T^2$ these are the area $A = \sqrt{\det g}$ and the complex modulus $\tau = (g_{12} + i\sqrt{\det g})/g_{11}$
in the upper half-plane, the shape of the lattice $\mathbb{Z} + \tau\mathbb{Z}$ (@exm-vcp-cy-torus).
:::

The moduli of a Calabi-Yau threefold are counted by its Hodge numbers. In type IIB string theory the dilaton and the
Ramond-Ramond axion add one more complex modulus.

::: {#exm-vcp-modulus-cy}
#### Moduli of a Calabi-Yau compactification

The quintic has $h^{1,1} = 1$ Kähler and $h^{2,1} = 101$ complex-structure moduli (@exm-vcp-hodge-moduli). Type IIB string
theory adds the axio-dilaton $\tau = C_0 + ie^{-\phi}$ [@grana2005, eq. 5.25], whose imaginary part is the inverse
string coupling: the strength of the interactions is itself a modulus.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The overall scale of a Ricci-flat metric is a modulus because rescaling preserves Ricci-flatness. The first exercise
checks the scaling of the curvature with Sage.

::: {#exr-vcp-modulus-scaling}
#### Rescaling the metric with Sage

Show with Sage that $g \mapsto \lambda g$ leaves the Ricci tensor unchanged and divides the scalar curvature by
$\lambda$, on the sphere of radius $r$ and on a flat torus with a constant non-diagonal metric. Why is the size of a
sphere not a modulus of the vacuum equations, while the size of a torus is?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The Christoffel symbols are invariant under constant rescaling, hence so are the Riemann and Ricci tensors, and $R =
g^{mn}R_{mn}$ scales as $1/\lambda$. On the sphere $R_{mn} \ne 0$, so the sphere does not solve $R_{mn} = 0$ for any
radius, and in a theory where it does solve the equations (with flux, @prp-vcp-flux-minimum) the radius is fixed. On the
torus $R_{mn} = 0$ for every $\lambda$:

{{< sage exr-vcp-modulus-scaling >}}
:::

A torus compactification of string theory has moduli from the metric and from the antisymmetric tensor field $B_{mn}$.
The second exercise counts them.

::: {#exr-vcp-modulus-count}
#### Moduli of $T^6$

Count the moduli of a string compactification on $T^6$ from the constant metric and the constant two-form $B_{mn}$, and
explain why a constant $B$ is a flat direction.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The metric gives $6 \cdot 7/2 = 21$ moduli and $B_{mn}$ gives $\binom62 = 15$, together $36$. The action depends on $B$
only through $H = dB$, which vanishes for constant $B$, so constant values of $B$ cost no energy: they are flat
directions, the axions. Together they parametrise $SO(6, 6)/(SO(6) \times SO(6))$, of dimension $66 - 30 = 36$.
:::

A light modulus is a new long-range force. The third exercise converts a range into a mass bound. The answer is the origin of the bound in @def-vcp-modulus.

::: {#exr-vcp-modulus-force}
#### A fifth force

A scalar of mass $m$ coupled to matter with gravitational strength changes Newton's potential to $-\frac{Gm_1m_2}{r}(1 +
\alpha e^{-mr})$ with $\alpha$ of order one. If Newton's law holds down to $r = 0.1$ mm, what is the smallest allowed $m$?
Compare with the bound quoted in @def-vcp-modulus.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The correction is invisible when $e^{-mr}$ is small at the shortest distance tested, $m \gtrsim 1/r$. With $\hbar c = 1.
97 \times 10^{-7}$ eV m, $1/(0.1\text{ mm}) = 1.97 \times 10^{-7}/10^{-4}$ eV $\approx 2 \times 10^{-3}$ eV, the
order of magnitude of the bound $10^{-3}$ eV [@douglas2006, Sec. I]. Moduli with a potential of the size produced by
fluxes are far heavier.
:::
::::

### Flux quantisation

A field strength whose integral over a closed surface is non-zero cannot be written as $dA$ with a global potential,
just as the field of a magnetic monopole cannot. Quantum mechanics then forces the integral to be a multiple of a
fixed unit.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcp-flux-quantum}
#### Flux quantum

Let $F$ be a closed $p$-form field strength on the internal space $X$ (locally $F = dA$) and $\Sigma \subset X$ a closed
$p$-dimensional submanifold, a $p$-cycle. The **flux** of $F$ through $\Sigma$ is $\int_\Sigma F$, which depends only on
the homology class of $\Sigma$. For a two-form coupled to particles of charge $q$, consistency of the wave functions
requires
$$
\int_\Sigma F \in \frac{2\pi}{q}\mathbb{Z} ,
$$ {#eq-vcp-flux-quantisation}
and the integer is the number of **flux quanta**. In string theory every flux with a standard Bianchi identity obeys
$\frac{1}{(2\pi\sqrt{\alpha'})^{p-1}}\int_\Sigma F_p \in \mathbb{Z}$ [@grana2005, eq. 2.5], so a flux configuration is a
vector of integers $n_i = \int_{\Sigma_i}F$ over a basis of cycles [@douglas2006, eqs. 11-12].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The magnetic monopole on the sphere is the prototype. Its flux is quantised by Dirac's argument, which the
proposition below repeats on a sphere of any radius.

::: {#exm-vcp-flux-monopole}
#### The monopole

The potential $A = g\cos\theta\,d\varphi$ on $S^2$ has $\int F = 4\pi g$ in magnitude, and a field of charge $q$ is
single valued only if $2qg \in \mathbb{Z}$ (@exr-dirac-quantisation): the flux is $2\pi N/q$ with $N = 2qg$, as in
@eq-vcp-flux-quantisation.
:::

A constant field on a torus is the simplest flux on a flat space. It is quantised by the same argument applied to
the periodicity of the torus.

::: {#exm-vcp-flux-torus}
#### Flux on a torus

On the torus $[0, L_1] \times [0, L_2]$ with periodic identifications, $F = f\,dx \wedge dy$ with constant $f$ is closed,
and $\int_{T^2}F = fL_1L_2$. Quantisation demands $qfL_1L_2 = 2\pi N$ (@exr-vcp-flux-torus): the field strength of $N$ flux
quanta falls as the inverse area.
:::

Type IIB string theory has two three-form field strengths, and a Calabi-Yau threefold has $b_3 = 2h^{2,1} + 2$
independent three-cycles. Each choice of fluxes is a vector of integers.

::: {#exm-vcp-flux-iib}
#### Three-form fluxes

The fluxes of $H_3$ and $F_3$ through a symplectic basis $A_K, B^K$ of three-cycles are integers $(m^K, e_K)$ and $(m^K_{RR},
e_{RR\,K})$, $K = 1, \dots, h^{2,1} + 1$ [@grana2005, eq. 2.6]. They carry the charge of D3-branes, $N_{\rm flux} = e_Km^K_{RR} -
m^Ke_{RR\,K}$, which must cancel against branes and orientifold planes [@grana2005, eqs. 4.21-4.22]: the integers
are bounded.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise derives @exm-vcp-flux-torus from the periodicity of the gauge potential. It is the torus version of
the Dirac argument.

::: {#exr-vcp-flux-torus}
#### Quantisation on a torus with Sage

With $A = fx\,dy$ on the torus, compute $A(x + L_1) - A(x)$, write it as the derivative of a gauge function, and show with
Sage that the gauge transformation is single valued in $y$ exactly when $qfL_1L_2 \in 2\pi\mathbb{Z}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$A(x + L_1) - A(x) = fL_1\,dy = d(fL_1y)$, a gauge transformation by $e^{iqfL_1y}$, which must return to itself under $y
\mapsto y + L_2$: $e^{iqfL_1L_2} = 1$. The flux is then $2\pi N/q$; for $N = \tfrac12$ the transition function flips sign:

{{< sage exr-vcp-flux-torus >}}
:::

Flux quanta are topological invariants of a line bundle. The second exercise makes the connection with the Chern
number of Part I.

::: {#exr-vcp-flux-chern}
#### Flux as a Chern number

Explain why the integer $N$ in @eq-vcp-flux-quantisation is the first Chern number of the line bundle on which the charged
fields live (@def-chern-number), and identify the bundle for $N = 1$ on the sphere.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
A charged field is a section of a complex line bundle whose transition functions are the gauge transformations
relating the potentials on overlapping patches. The curvature of the connection $d + iqA$ is $iqF$, so the first Chern
number is $\frac{q}{2\pi}\int F = N$, an integer that cannot change under continuous deformations.
For $N = 1$ on $S^2$ the bundle is the one associated with the Hopf fibration $S^3 \to S^2$
(@exm-hopf-connection-monopole); in Kaluza-Klein language the flux counts how many times the circle is twisted over
the sphere.
:::

Integers bounded by a tadpole condition make a large but finite set. The third exercise estimates its size for the
quintic.

::: {#exr-vcp-flux-count}
#### How many flux integers

For type IIB on the quintic, how many integers specify $H_3$ and $F_3$? The tadpole condition reads $N_{\rm flux} \le L$
for some $L$ fixed by the orientifold. Is the set of allowed fluxes finite?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$b_3 = 204$, so $H_3$ and $F_3$ give $408$ integers. The condition $N_{\rm flux} \le L$ is a single quadratic
inequality in them, and the quadratic form $e_Km^K_{RR} - m^Ke_{RR\,K}$ is indefinite, so by itself it does not bound the
integers. Finiteness comes from combining it with the minimisation conditions and the identification of fluxes
related by duality transformations, as in the rigid example of @exm-vcp-landscape-rigid, where the count is $2\sigma(L)$;
the estimates of @def-vcp-landscape follow [@douglas2006, Sec. V].
:::
::::

The sphere is the internal space of the one-modulus model below. On it Dirac's argument is a short computation with
the two patch potentials.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-vcp-dirac-flux}
#### Dirac quantisation on a two-sphere

On the sphere of radius $R$ let $F = \frac{N}{2qR^2}\,\mathrm{vol}$, $\mathrm{vol} = R^2\sin\theta\,d\theta \wedge d\varphi$. Then
$\int_{S^2}F = 2\pi N/q$; the potentials $A_\pm = \frac{N}{2q}(\pm1 - \cos\theta)\,d\varphi$, regular at the north and south
pole, both satisfy $dA_\pm = F$ and differ by $A_+ - A_- = \frac Nq\,d\varphi$; the transition function $e^{iN\varphi}$ is
single valued exactly for $N \in \mathbb{Z}$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Checked by exact computation in `figures/flux_potential.sage`.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The smallest flux is a single quantum. Its bundle is the one that turns the sphere into the three-sphere. It is also the simplest example of a non-trivial bundle.

::: {#exm-vcp-dirac-hopf}
#### One quantum

$N = 1$ is the Hopf monopole: the circle bundle with transition function $e^{i\varphi}$ is $S^3 \to S^2$
(@def-hopf-connection), and a charge-$q$ field on the sphere is a section of the associated line bundle. $N = 0$ is the
trivial bundle, $S^2 \times S^1$.
:::

The same integer appears in Kaluza-Klein charge quantisation. There the charges of the modes on a circle are
multiples of a unit fixed by the radius.

::: {#exm-vcp-dirac-kk}
#### Relation with Kaluza-Klein charges

In Part III the charges of the Kaluza-Klein modes are multiples of a unit fixed by the radius
(@def-charge-quantisation), because $e^{iny/R}$ must be periodic. Dirac quantisation is the same requirement of single
valuedness applied to the transition functions of a bundle, and a monopole background on the base of a Kaluza-Klein
circle bundle is exactly a twisted circle with $N$ quanta of twist.
:::

The field strength of a fixed number of quanta decreases as the sphere grows. Its energy therefore depends on the
radius, which is how fluxes act on moduli.

::: {#exm-vcp-dirac-dilution}
#### Dilution

The magnitude $\frac{N}{2qR^2}$ of the field falls as $R^{-2}$ while the area grows as $R^2$, so the Maxwell energy
$\tfrac14\int F_{mn}F^{mn}\,\mathrm{vol} = \frac{\pi N^2}{2q^2R^2}$ (@exr-vcp-dirac-energy) decreases as the sphere grows: the
flux pushes the radius outwards, and something else (the curvature, @prp-vcp-flux-minimum) must pull it back.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise computes the energy of the flux. The answer is the flux term of the potential before the
conversion to four-dimensional Einstein frame.

::: {#exr-vcp-dirac-energy}
#### The energy of the flux with Sage

For $F$ as in @prp-vcp-dirac-flux compute $F_{mn}F^{mn}$ and $\tfrac14\int_{S^2}F_{mn}F^{mn}\,\mathrm{vol}$ with Sage.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$F_{mn}F^{mn} = N^2/(2q^2R^4)$, constant on the sphere, and the energy is $\pi N^2/(2q^2R^2)$, quadratic in the number of
quanta:

{{< sage exr-vcp-dirac-energy >}}
:::

Half-integer fluxes are not allowed for charge-$q$ fields, but they can be for fields of other charges. The second
exercise examines what goes wrong.

::: {#exr-vcp-dirac-half}
#### Half a quantum

Take $N = \tfrac12$ in @prp-vcp-dirac-flux. What happens to a field of charge $q$, and to one of charge $2q$? What does this
say about the relation between the smallest charge in a theory and the allowed fluxes?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For charge $q$ the transition function is $e^{i\varphi/2}$, which changes sign under $\varphi \to \varphi + 2\pi$: the field
cannot be defined on the overlap and the configuration is inconsistent. For charge $2q$ it is $e^{i\varphi}$, single
valued. The allowed fluxes are fixed by the smallest charge present: a single field of charge $q$ is enough to forbid
$N \notin \mathbb{Z}$, Dirac's argument for charge quantisation run in reverse.
:::

Fluxes of higher-degree forms are quantised the same way with the string-theory normalisation. The third exercise
computes a three-form flux on a three-sphere.

::: {#exr-vcp-dirac-three-form}
#### A three-form flux

A uniform three-form $H = h\,\mathrm{vol}_{S^3}$ on the three-sphere of radius $R$, of volume $2\pi^2R^3$, obeys
$\frac{1}{(2\pi\sqrt{\alpha'})^2}\int_{S^3}H \in \mathbb{Z}$ [@grana2005, eq. 2.5]. Find $h$ for $N$ quanta and the radius
dependence of the energy $\int H \wedge *H$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$2\pi^2R^3h = 4\pi^2\alpha'N$ gives $h = 2\alpha'N/R^3$, and $\int H \wedge *H = h^2 \cdot 2\pi^2R^3 = 8\pi^2\alpha'^2N^2/R^3$:
again quadratic in $N$ and decreasing with the radius, faster than the two-form energy because the field spreads over
three dimensions.
:::
::::

### The flux potential

After reduction the flux energy becomes a term in the four-dimensional potential of the moduli. Combined with the
curvature of the internal space it can have a minimum, which fixes the moduli.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcp-flux-potential}
#### Flux potential

The **flux potential** is the energy of the fluxes, $V_{\rm flux} \propto \int_X F \wedge *F$ [@douglas2006, eq. 13],
regarded as a function of the moduli: the fluxes are fixed integers, so the field strengths, and their energy, depend
on the metric of $X$. In four-dimensional Einstein frame (@def-einstein-frame) it adds to the potential produced by the
internal curvature. For six-dimensional Einstein-Maxwell theory on $M_4 \times S^2$ with $N$ flux quanta and sphere
radius $R$ the result is the one-modulus potential
$$
V(R) = \frac{aN^2}{R^6} - \frac{b}{R^4}, \qquad a, b > 0
$$ {#eq-vcp-flux-potential}
[@douglas2006, eq. 17], the first term from the flux and the second from the positive curvature of the sphere.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
