![Left: the one-modulus flux potential @eq-vcp-flux-potential with $a = b = 1$ for $N = 1, 2, 3$ flux quanta, scaled by
$N^4$, with the minima at $R = \sqrt{3/2}\,N$ marked; all three have the same depth $-4/27$ after scaling. Right: a
two-flux landscape in the manner of Bousso and Polchinski, $V = -60 + n_1^2 + \sqrt5\,n_2^2$ over the integers $(n_1, n_2)$;
the dark points have $V < 0$, the light ones $V > 0$, and the eight red points between the dashed ellipses have $|V| < 1$.
Generated by `figures/flux_potential.sage`.](figures/flux_potential.svg){#fig-flux-potential width=95%}

{{< interactive flux_potential 460 >}}

The powers of $R$ in @eq-vcp-flux-potential come from three sources. The example traces them. Two of them are geometric and one comes from the change of frame.

::: {#exm-vcp-fluxpot-scalings}
#### Where the powers come from

The flux energy density $\propto N^2/R^4$ (@exm-vcp-dirac-dilution) integrates over the area $4\pi R^2$ to $\propto
N^2/R^2$; the curvature term $-\int\sqrt\gamma\,R_{\rm int} = -4\pi R^2 \cdot 2/R^2$ is independent of $R$. Rescaling the
four-dimensional metric to Einstein frame, to remove the factor $R^2$ multiplying the four-dimensional curvature, divides
every potential term by $(R^2)^2$: hence $N^2/R^6$ and $-1/R^4$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** The scalings are checked in `figures/flux_potential.sage`.
:::

In type IIB string theory the three-form fluxes produce a superpotential. It depends on some moduli and not on others,
which decides what is stabilised.

::: {#exm-vcp-fluxpot-gvw}
#### The flux superpotential

Type IIB fluxes give the superpotential $W = \int_X G_3 \wedge \Omega$, $G_3 = F_3 - \tau H_3$ [@grana2005, eq. 5.43;
@douglas2006, eq. 59], which depends on the complex-structure moduli through $\Omega$ and on the axio-dilaton $\tau$, but
not on the Kähler moduli. The resulting potential is positive semi-definite and vanishes at its minima, fixing the
complex structure and $\tau$ while the overall volume stays a flat direction [@grana2005, eq. 5.46; @douglas2006,
eqs. 62-63].
:::

The volume needs an effect beyond fluxes. Non-perturbative effects add an exponential to the superpotential, the KKLT
construction. The result is the simplest model in which every modulus is fixed.

::: {#exm-vcp-fluxpot-kklt}
#### KKLT

With one Kähler modulus $T$, Kähler potential $K = -3\log(T + \bar T)$ and superpotential $W = W_0 + Be^{-2\pi T}$ ($W_0$
the flux superpotential at its minimum), the condition $D_TW = 0$ at real $T = \sigma$ gives $W_0 = -Be^{-2\pi\sigma}(1 +
\tfrac{4\pi}{3}\sigma)$ and an anti-de Sitter minimum $V = -\frac{2\pi^2B^2e^{-4\pi\sigma}}{3\sigma}$ [@grana2005, eqs. 7.
7-7.9], at large volume when $|W_0|$ is small (@exr-vcp-fluxpot-kklt). Anti-D3 branes add $D/\sigma^3$ and can lift the
minimum to a metastable de Sitter vacuum [@grana2005, eqs. 7.10-7.11].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise solves the KKLT condition. It is an equation in one real variable once the axion is set to zero.

::: {#exr-vcp-fluxpot-kklt}
#### The KKLT minimum with Sage

With $K$ and $W$ as in @exm-vcp-fluxpot-kklt, compute $D_TW = \partial_TW + (\partial_TK)W$ at $T = \sigma$ with Sage, solve
$D_TW = 0$ for $W_0$, check $V = -3e^K|W|^2$ at the solution, and find $\sigma$ for $B = 1$ and $W_0 = -10^{-4}, -10^{-8}, -
10^{-12}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\partial_TK = -3/(2\sigma)$ gives $W_0 = -Be^{-2\pi\sigma}(1 + 4\pi\sigma/3)$ and $V = -2\pi^2B^2e^{-4\pi\sigma}/(3\sigma)$. The
solutions $\sigma \approx 1.8, 3.4, 4.9$ grow like $\log(1/|W_0|)$: a small flux superpotential gives a large volume,
which is what makes the approximation trustworthy:

{{< sage exr-vcp-fluxpot-kklt >}}
:::

The flatness of the volume direction in @exm-vcp-fluxpot-gvw is an exact cancellation in supergravity. The second
exercise exhibits it. It explains why fluxes alone leave the volume undetermined.

::: {#exr-vcp-fluxpot-noscale}
#### No-scale structure with Sage

For $K = -3\log(T + \bar T)$ show with Sage that $K^{T\bar T}K_TK_{\bar T} = 3$, and conclude that $V = e^K(K^{T\bar T}|D_TW|^2 -
3|W|^2)$ vanishes identically for any constant $W$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$K_T = -3/(T + \bar T)$ and $K_{T\bar T} = 3/(T + \bar T)^2$, so $K^{T\bar T}K_TK_{\bar T} = 3$; for constant $W$, $D_TW = K_TW$
and the two terms cancel. A constant flux superpotential leaves the volume exactly flat, the **no-scale** property
[@grana2005, Sec. 5.2]:

{{< sage exr-vcp-fluxpot-noscale >}}
:::

Not every internal space can be stabilised by flux alone. The third exercise shows what happens without the
curvature term.

::: {#exr-vcp-fluxpot-runaway}
#### Runaway on a torus

Repeat the derivation of @eq-vcp-flux-potential for $T^2$ instead of $S^2$, and for a Riemann surface of genus $g \ge 2$
with its constant negative curvature metric. Does the radius have a minimum?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
On $T^2$ the curvature vanishes, $b = 0$, and $V = aN^2/R^6$ decreases monotonically: the torus decompactifies. On a
surface of genus $g \ge 2$ the Gauss-Bonnet integral $\int\sqrt\gamma R_{\rm int} = 4\pi\chi = 8\pi(1 - g)$ is negative, so
the curvature term changes sign, $b < 0$, and $V = aN^2/R^6 + |b|/R^4$ again decreases monotonically. Only positive
curvature, $\chi > 0$, gives the competition that produces a minimum.
:::
::::

The minimum of the one-modulus potential can be found in closed form. The proposition records it together with the
sign of the second derivative.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-vcp-flux-minimum}
#### Stabilisation of the radius

For $a, b, N > 0$ the potential @eq-vcp-flux-potential has exactly one critical point on $R > 0$,
$$
R_{\min}^2 = \frac{3aN^2}{2b}, \qquad V(R_{\min}) = -\frac{4b^3}{27a^2N^4} < 0, \qquad V''(R_{\min}) = \frac{64b^4}{27a^3N^6} > 0 ,
$$ {#eq-vcp-flux-minimum}
and it is the global minimum, since $V \to +\infty$ as $R \to 0$ and $V \to 0^-$ as $R \to \infty$. The flux fixes the radius
at a value proportional to $N$, in an anti-de Sitter vacuum.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Checked by exact computation in `figures/flux_potential.sage`, together with the scalings of the two terms.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Large fluxes give large radii. That is the regime in which the supergravity approximation is valid. It is the regime in which the computation can be trusted.

::: {#exm-vcp-fluxmin-large-n}
#### Large flux, large radius

$R_{\min} = \sqrt{3a/2b}\,N$ grows linearly with the number of quanta, so moderately large $N$ produces a radius large in
fundamental units and small curvatures, "justifying the use of supergravity" [@douglas2006, Sec. II.D.1]. The depth of the
minimum falls as $N^{-4}$ (@fig-flux-potential).
:::

The vacuum energy at the minimum is negative. Its size is comparable to the internal curvature, which limits the use
of the model as a four-dimensional effective theory.

::: {#exm-vcp-fluxmin-ads}
#### Anti-de Sitter and scale separation

$V(R_{\min}) < 0$ is a negative cosmological constant (@def-cosmological-constant): spacetime is anti-de Sitter, as in the
Freund-Rubin solutions of @def-freund-rubin-ansatz. Its curvature radius is of the same order as the radius of the sphere,
so there is no regime in which the four-dimensional curvature is small compared to the Kaluza-Klein masses
[@douglas2006, Sec. II.D.1] (@exr-vcp-fluxmin-mass).
:::

Adding a positive constant lifts the minimum without moving it. This is a cartoon of the uplift that turns the KKLT
minimum into a de Sitter vacuum.

::: {#exm-vcp-fluxmin-uplift}
#### Uplift

$V + \epsilon$ with a constant $\epsilon > 0$ has the same minimum at $R_{\min}$ and the value $\epsilon - 4b^3/(27a^2N^4)$,
positive for $\epsilon > 4b^3/(27a^2N^4)$: a de Sitter vacuum. In this cartoon the potential tends to $\epsilon$ at large
$R$, above the minimum, so the vacuum is stable. A realistic uplift decays with the volume, like the $D/\sigma^3$ of KKLT;
the potential then tends to zero at large volume, below the de Sitter minimum, which is therefore only metastable,
with decompactification as the decay channel [@grana2005, Sec. 7.4].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The structure of @prp-vcp-flux-minimum does not depend on the precise exponents. The first exercise proves the general
version. Any pair of powers with the flux term falling faster gives a minimum.

::: {#exr-vcp-fluxmin-general}
#### Other exponents with Sage

Let $V = aN^2/R^p - b/R^q$ with $p > q > 0$. Find the critical point with Sage, show that it is a minimum with
$V''(R_m) = qb(p - q)R_m^{-q-2}$ and $V(R_m) = -b(1 - q/p)R_m^{-q}$, and evaluate it for $(p, q) = (6, 4), (4, 2), (3, 1)$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$R_m^{p-q} = paN^2/(qb)$. At this point $paN^2R_m^{-p} = qbR_m^{-q}$, which gives both formulas; for $(6, 4)$ they reproduce
@eq-vcp-flux-minimum:

{{< sage exr-vcp-fluxmin-general >}}
:::

The mass of the stabilised modulus can be compared with the Kaluza-Klein masses. The second exercise does the
comparison by powers of $N$.

::: {#exr-vcp-fluxmin-mass}
#### Modulus mass and Kaluza-Klein scale

The Einstein-frame kinetic term of the radius is $c\,(\partial\log R)^2$ with $c$ of order one. Show that the modulus mass
satisfies $m_R^2 \sim R^2V''(R_{\min})$, and compare its dependence on $N$ with $|V(R_{\min})|$ and with the Kaluza-Klein masses
$m_{KK}^2 \sim R^{-2}$ in six-dimensional units, which become $R^{-4}$ in Einstein frame.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $\rho = \log R$, $\partial_\rho^2V = R^2V''$ at a critical point, so $m_R^2 = R^2V''(R_{\min})/2c = \frac{3aN^2}{2b} \cdot
\frac{64b^4}{27a^3N^6}/2c = \frac{16b^3}{9a^2N^4c} \propto N^{-4}$. The vacuum energy $|V(R_{\min})| \propto N^{-4}$ and $m_{KK}^2
\propto R^{-4} \propto N^{-4}$ scale the same way: all three scales are comparable for every $N$, which is the lack of scale
separation of @exm-vcp-fluxmin-ads.
:::

The constants $a$ and $b$ must have definite signs for a minimum to exist. The third exercise collects the cases.

::: {#exr-vcp-fluxmin-signs}
#### Signs

Find when $V = aN^2/R^6 - b/R^4$ has a minimum on $R > 0$ for all signs of $a$ and $b$, and interpret each case.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$V' = R^{-7}(-6aN^2 + 4bR^2)$ vanishes for $R^2 = 3aN^2/(2b)$, which needs $a$ and $b$ of the same sign; then $V'' = 64b^4/(27a^3N^6)$
has the sign of $a$. So a minimum requires $a > 0$ (positive flux energy, always true) and $b > 0$ (positive internal
curvature). For $a > 0 > b$ the potential decreases monotonically to $0$ (runaway, @exr-vcp-fluxpot-runaway); for $a < 0$
the energy would be unbounded below, which a physical flux never gives.
:::
::::

### The landscape

Each choice of flux integers gives its own minimum, with its own vacuum energy. The number of choices is so large that
the vacua form an almost continuous spectrum of cosmological constants.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcp-landscape}
#### Flux landscape

The **flux landscape** of a compactification is the set of its vacua as the flux integers $n_1, \dots, n_K$ range over
the values allowed by the tadpole condition. In the model of Bousso and Polchinski the vacuum energy is $V = -V_0 +
\sum_ic_in_i^2$ with $\sum_in_i^2 \le L$, so the vacua are the lattice points of a $K$-dimensional ball of radius $\sqrt L$,
about
$$
N_{\rm vac} \approx \frac{\pi^{K/2}L^{K/2}}{\Gamma(K/2 + 1)}
$$ {#eq-vcp-landscape-count}
of them, and those with small $|V|$ lie in a thin shell; $K = 100$, $L = 100$ gives $10^{60}$ [@douglas2006, eqs. 18-20].
For type IIB string theory on Calabi-Yau orientifolds the estimates are of order $10^{500}$ [@douglas2006, Sec. V.D.4].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The shell of small vacuum energy is visible already with two fluxes. The right panel of @fig-flux-potential shows it. The red points of the figure are the nearly flat vacua.

::: {#exm-vcp-landscape-shell}
#### A two-flux shell

With $V = -60 + n_1^2 + \sqrt5\,n_2^2$ the vacua with $|V| < 1$ are the eight integer points between the ellipses $n_1^2 +
\sqrt5n_2^2 = 59$ and $61$ (@fig-flux-potential). With $\sqrt5$ irrational no two vacua have the same energy, and in higher
dimensions the shell contains a fraction of all points proportional to its thickness.
:::

A huge number of vacua spread over a finite range of energies leaves a tiny spacing. This is the landscape's answer to
the smallness of the observed cosmological constant.

::: {#exm-vcp-landscape-spacing}
#### The spacing of vacuum energies

$N_{\rm vac}$ vacua with energies spread over a range of order $V_0$ have a typical spacing $V_0/N_{\rm vac}$. With
$10^{500}$ vacua and $V_0$ of order the Planck scale, some vacua have $|\Lambda|$ as small as the observed $10^{-120}$ in
Planck units [@douglas2006, Sec. II.E]. Which vacuum is realised is not explained by this counting.
:::

On a rigid Calabi-Yau manifold the only modulus is the axio-dilaton, and the vacua can be counted exactly. The count
involves the divisor function.

::: {#exm-vcp-landscape-rigid}
#### A rigid Calabi-Yau

With $h^{2,1} = 0$ the superpotential is linear in $\tau$, $W = F\tau + G$ with $F$, $G$ integer combinations of the
fluxes, and $D_\tau W = 0$ gives $\bar\tau = -G/F$ [@douglas2006, eq. 154]. Counting the solutions up to $SL(2, \mathbb{Z})$
gives $2\sigma(L)$ vacua for tadpole $L$, $\sigma(L)$ the sum of the divisors of $L$ [@douglas2006, eq. 157].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The volume formula @eq-vcp-landscape-count approximates a lattice count. The first exercise tests the approximation in
low dimensions. The comparison shows how good the continuum approximation is.

::: {#exr-vcp-landscape-ball}
#### Lattice points in balls with Sage

Count the points of $\mathbb{Z}^d$ with $|n|^2 \le 400$ for $d = 1, \dots, 5$ with Sage and compare with the volume of the ball;
then evaluate @eq-vcp-landscape-count for $K = L = 100$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The ratios are $1.025$, $1.000$, $0.997$, $1.000$, $1.004$: the volume is an excellent estimate once the radius is large
compared to the lattice spacing. For $K = L = 100$, $\pi^{50}10^{100}/50! \approx 2.4 \times 10^{60}$:

{{< sage exr-vcp-landscape-ball >}}
:::

The exact count on a rigid Calabi-Yau has a simple asymptotic form. The second exercise checks it. The divisor sums can be computed directly in Sage.

::: {#exr-vcp-landscape-rigid}
#### Counting rigid vacua with Sage

Compute $\sum_{L \le L_{\max}}2\sigma(L)$ for $L_{\max} = 10^3$ and $10^4$ with Sage and compare with $\frac{\pi^2}{6}L_{\max}^2$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The ratios are $1.0007$ and $1.0001$: the number of vacua with tadpole up to $L_{\max}$ grows like $L_{\max}^2$, in
agreement with $\sum_{L \le N}\sigma(L) = \frac{\pi^2}{12}N^2 + O(N\log N)$ [@douglas2006, Sec. V.B.1]:

{{< sage exr-vcp-landscape-rigid >}}
:::

How many vacua have nearly vanishing vacuum energy depends on the thickness of the shell. The third exercise estimates
the fraction.

::: {#exr-vcp-landscape-fraction}
#### The fraction of nearly flat vacua

In the Bousso-Polchinski model with all $c_i = c$, estimate the fraction of vacua with $|V| < \epsilon$ when $V_0 \gg
\epsilon$, using the volume of a thin spherical shell.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|V| < \epsilon$ means $V_0 - \epsilon < c|n|^2 < V_0 + \epsilon$: a shell between radii $\sqrt{(V_0 \mp \epsilon)/c}$, of
volume $\approx \frac{d}{dr}(\Omega_Kr^K)\,\delta r = K\Omega_Kr^{K-1}\delta r$ with $r = \sqrt{V_0/c}$ and $\delta r = \epsilon/\sqrt{cV_0}$.
Relative to the ball $|n|^2 \le L$, of volume $\Omega_KL^{K/2}$, the fraction is $\frac{K\epsilon}{V_0}\left(\frac{V_0}{cL}\right)^{K/2}$: linear in $\epsilon$, so
the energies of the vacua are spread almost uniformly near zero.
:::
::::

Not all fluxes are field strengths on a manifold. Applying T-duality to a torus with $H$-flux gives a twisted torus,
whose "geometric flux" $f^a{}_{bc}$ measures the twisting of the circle fibres and must be integral; a second T-duality
gives a space that is only locally geometric, glued by transformations that mix the metric with the $B$-field and
characterised by a **non-geometric flux** $Q^{ab}{}_c$; a third, more conjectural, gives an $R$-flux with no local
geometric description at all [@wecht2007, Secs. 1, 3.1 and 4]. In the four-dimensional theory all these fluxes appear on
the same footing, as structure constants of the gauge group of a gauged supergravity, so that a general gauged
supergravity is expected to lift to a non-geometric compactification [@wecht2007, Sec. 5.1]. The Scherk-Schwarz and
group-manifold reductions of @sec-vi-torus-scherk-schwarz and @sec-vi-group-manifolds are the geometric part of this
picture.

## Warped and large extra dimensions {#sec-vi-warped}

The compactifications so far are products, $M_4 \times X$, with $X$ small, of order the Planck or string length. Two
proposals give up one of these assumptions to explain why gravity is so much weaker than the other forces. In the
Randall-Sundrum model the four-dimensional metric is multiplied by a warp factor that depends exponentially on the
extra coordinate, and masses on a brane at the far end are red-shifted by that factor. In the model of Arkani-Hamed,
Dimopoulos and Dvali the extra dimensions are large, up to a millimetre, and the Planck mass is large because the
volume is. This section solves the five-dimensional Einstein equations for the warped metric, finds the graviton
that is localised near the brane, and computes the sizes required of large extra dimensions.

### The Randall-Sundrum metric

The fifth dimension of the Randall-Sundrum model is an interval, the orbifold $S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$ of
@exm-vcp-orbifold-interval, with a three-brane at each end. The metric is not a product: the scale of the
four-dimensional slices changes along the fifth dimension.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcp-rs-metric}
#### Randall-Sundrum metric

On $M_4 \times S^1/\mathbb{Z}_2$, with $y \in [-\pi r_c, \pi r_c]$ and $y \sim -y$, the **Randall-Sundrum metric** is
$$
ds^2 = e^{-2k|y|}\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - dy^2 ,
$$ {#eq-vcp-rs-metric}
in the signature $(+, -, -, -, -)$, with a constant $k > 0$. The function $e^{-2k|y|}$ is the **warp factor**. Three-branes
sit at the fixed points $y = 0$ and $y = \pi r_c$, and the five-dimensional bulk has a negative cosmological constant.
@randall1999a [eqs. 6 and 12] write the metric in the signature $(-, +, +, +, +)$ with $y = r_c\phi$, and
@randall1999b [eq. 4] take $r_c \to \infty$ with a single brane at $y = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
Proper energies at different $y$ are measured with different four-dimensional metrics. A mass parameter on the brane
at $y$ appears red-shifted when measured with the metric of the brane at $y = 0$.

::: {#exm-vcp-rs-redshift}
#### Red-shift along the fifth dimension

The induced metric on the slice at fixed $y$ is $e^{-2k|y|}\eta_{\mu\nu}$, so a field theory on the slice with mass
parameter $m_0$ is, in terms of the coordinates $x^\mu$ normalised at $y = 0$, a theory with mass $e^{-k|y|}m_0$. At $y =
\pi r_c$ the factor is $e^{-k r_c\pi}$, which is the hierarchy of @exm-vcp-rssol-hierarchy.
:::

A change of coordinate makes the metric conformally flat. In that form the bulk is recognisably a piece of
anti-de Sitter space.

::: {#exm-vcp-rs-ads}
#### Conformal coordinates

For $y > 0$ let $z = (e^{ky} - 1)/k$. Then $e^{-2ky} = (1 + kz)^{-2}$ and $dy = dz/(1 + kz)$, so @eq-vcp-rs-metric becomes
$(1 + k|z|)^{-2}(\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - dz^2)$ (@exr-vcp-rs-conformal), the Poincaré patch of five-dimensional
anti-de Sitter space of radius $1/k$ in the coordinate $|z| + 1/k$, with the region next to its boundary cut away
(@exm-vcp-adsq-rs): the bulk is "a slice of an $AdS_5$ geometry"
[@randall1999a, Sec. 3].
:::

With the second brane removed to infinity the extra dimension is infinite. Gravity nevertheless remains
four-dimensional at long distances, as @def-vcp-graviton-zero-mode explains.

::: {#exm-vcp-rs-single-brane}
#### One brane and an infinite dimension

For $r_c \to \infty$ the metric @eq-vcp-rs-metric covers $y \in \mathbb{R}$ with a single brane at $y = 0$
[@randall1999b, eqs. 3-4]. The proper length of the fifth dimension is infinite, but its warped volume $\int e^{-2k|y|}dy =
1/k$ is finite, which is what makes the four-dimensional Planck mass finite (@prp-vcp-rs-solution).
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The conformal form of the metric follows from the change of variables. The first exercise checks it with Sage. Only the logarithm and the exponential are involved.

::: {#exr-vcp-rs-conformal}
#### Conformal coordinates with Sage

Verify with Sage that $z = (e^{ky} - 1)/k$ inverts to $y = \log(1 + kz)/k$, and that $e^{-2ky}$ and $(dy/dz)^2$ are both
$(1 + kz)^{-2}$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Both factors equal $(1 + kz)^{-2}$, so the four-dimensional part and the $dz^2$ part are multiplied by the same function:

{{< sage exr-vcp-rs-conformal >}}
:::

Anti-de Sitter space is maximally symmetric, with a Riemann tensor fixed by the metric. The second exercise computes
the curvature of the bulk with the conventions of the book.

::: {#exr-vcp-rs-ads-curvature}
#### The bulk is anti-de Sitter, with Sage

For $y > 0$ compute the Riemann tensor of @eq-vcp-rs-metric with Sage and show $R_{MNPQ} = k^2(g_{MP}g_{NQ} -
g_{MQ}g_{NP})$, $R_{MN} = 4k^2g_{MN}$, $R = 20k^2$. Which cosmological constant does @def-vacuum-solution assign to it?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
All components agree, and the vacuum equation $R_{MN} = -\tfrac{2\Lambda}{3}g_{MN}$ in five dimensions gives $\Lambda = -6k^2$:
in the signature $(+, -, -, -, -)$ a positive multiple of $g_{MN}$ in the Ricci tensor is the anti-de Sitter sign, as for
the four-dimensional anti-de Sitter factor of @def-freund-rubin-ansatz:

{{< sage exr-vcp-rs-ads-curvature >}}
:::

Without the warp factor the model reduces to the familiar circle. The third exercise takes the limit. The comparison shows what the warp factor adds.

::: {#exr-vcp-rs-flat-limit}
#### The limit $k \to 0$

Set $k = 0$ in @eq-vcp-rs-metric. What is the spectrum of a massless bulk scalar that is even under $y \to -y$, and how
does $M_{\rm Pl}$ depend on $r_c$? Compare with Part III.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For $k = 0$ the metric is the product $M_4 \times [0, \pi r_c]$. Even functions on the circle of radius $r_c$ are $\cos(ny/r_c)$,
$n \ge 0$, so the scalar gives the tower $m_n = n/r_c$ of @def-kk-mass with only the cosines kept. The Planck mass is
$M_{\rm Pl}^2 \propto M^3\pi r_c$, growing linearly with the size, the product-space relation [@randall1999b, p. 3] and the
analogue of @def-planck-radius-relation; the warp factor replaces $\pi r_c$ by $(1 - e^{-2kr_c\pi})/k$.
:::
::::

The conformal coordinates of @exm-vcp-rs-ads identified the bulk with a piece of anti-de Sitter space, and
@exr-vcp-rs-ads-curvature confirmed it by computing the curvature. Anti-de Sitter space has a description in which both
facts are visible before any Christoffel symbol is computed: it is a quadric in a flat space with two time directions,
just as the round spheres of the Freund-Rubin vacua are quadrics in Euclidean space (@exm-vcr-frg-quadric). The
proposition collects what follows from this picture in $D$ dimensions.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-vcp-ads-quadric}
#### Anti-de Sitter space as a quadric

Let $D \geq 2$ and $L > 0$, and let $\mathbb{R}^{2, D-1}$ carry the coordinates $X = (X^0, X^1, \dots, X^D)$ and the flat
metric with two time directions $X^0$ and $X^D$, written $X \cdot X = (X^0)^2 + (X^D)^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{D-1}(X^i)^2$. The
quadric
$$
AdS_D = \{X \in \mathbb{R}^{2, D-1} : X \cdot X = L^2\}
$$ {#eq-vcp-ads-quadric}
has the following properties [@boskoff2024journey, Secs. 11.2 and 12.5].

(i) Its unit normal $N = X/L$ has $N \cdot N = 1$, and its induced metric $g$ has the signature $(+, -, \dots, -)$. (The
quadric $X \cdot X = -L^2$ has signature $(2, D - 2)$ and is not a spacetime.)

(ii) Its second fundamental form is $h_{\mu\nu} = g_{\mu\nu}/L$, and the Gauss equation of a hypersurface in a flat space,
$R_{\rho\sigma\mu\nu} = (N \cdot N)(h_{\rho\mu}h_{\sigma\nu} - h_{\rho\nu}h_{\sigma\mu})$, gives
$$
R_{\rho\sigma\mu\nu} = \frac{1}{L^2}\left(g_{\rho\mu}g_{\sigma\nu} - g_{\rho\nu}g_{\sigma\mu}\right), \qquad R_{\mu\nu} =
\frac{D - 1}{L^2}g_{\mu\nu}, \qquad R = \frac{D(D - 1)}{L^2} .
$$ {#eq-vcp-ads-curvature}

(iii) It solves $R_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12Rg_{\mu\nu} = \Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$ with
$$
\Lambda = -\frac{(D - 1)(D - 2)}{2L^2} .
$$ {#eq-vcp-ads-lambda}

(iv) The group $SO(2, D - 1)$ of linear maps preserving $X \cdot X$ acts on it by isometries, with $D(D + 1)/2$ independent
Killing vectors: the space is maximally symmetric (@def-maximally-symmetric).

(v) On the half $X^D + X^{D-1} > 0$ the Poincaré coordinates $(x^\mu, w)$, $\mu = 0, \dots, D - 2$, $w > 0$, defined by
$X^\mu = Lx^\mu/w$, $X^D + X^{D-1} = L^2/w$ and $X^D - X^{D-1} = w - \eta_{\mu\nu}x^\mu x^\nu/w$, give
$$
ds^2 = \frac{L^2}{w^2}\left(\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - dw^2\right) .
$$ {#eq-vcp-ads-poincare}
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The Randall-Sundrum bulk is the case $D = 5$, and the Poincaré coordinate $w$ is an exponential of the coordinate $y$
of @eq-vcp-rs-metric. The first example makes the identification and locates the two branes on the quadric.

::: {#exm-vcp-adsq-rs}
#### The bulk of the Randall-Sundrum model

With $D = 5$, $L = 1/k$ and $w = e^{ky}/k$, @eq-vcp-ads-poincare becomes $e^{-2ky}\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - dy^2$
(@exr-vcp-adsq-poincare), the metric @eq-vcp-rs-metric for $y > 0$; the conformal coordinate of @exm-vcp-rs-ads is $z = w -
1/k$. The interval $0 \leq y \leq \pi r_c$ is the slab $1/k \leq w \leq e^{k\pi r_c}/k$: the hidden brane cuts away the part
$w < 1/k$ next to the boundary $w = 0$, the visible brane the part beyond it, and the orbifold glues two copies of the
slab along the branes. The cosmological constant @eq-vcp-ads-lambda is $\Lambda = -6k^2$, the value that
@prp-vcp-rs-solution derives below from the Einstein tensor.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The warp factor seems to make the points of the fifth dimension inequivalent, yet the bulk is maximally symmetric. The
second example resolves this: moving along $y$ is an isometry, and only the branes tell the slices apart.

::: {#exm-vcp-adsq-dilatation}
#### The hierarchy as an isometry

The boost $X^D \pm X^{D-1} \mapsto \lambda^{\mp1}(X^D \pm X^{D-1})$ of $\mathbb{R}^{2, D-1}$, mixing the second time with a
space direction, belongs to $SO(2, D - 1)$; in Poincaré coordinates it is the dilatation $(x^\mu, w) \mapsto (\lambda x^\mu,
\lambda w)$, which leaves @eq-vcp-ads-poincare unchanged. With $\lambda = e^{kc}$ it is $y \mapsto y + c$, $x^\mu \mapsto
e^{kc}x^\mu$ in the Randall-Sundrum coordinates (@exr-vcp-adsq-killing). All slices $y = \mathrm{const}$ are therefore
equivalent in the bulk, and the red-shift $e^{-k\pi r_c}$ of @exm-vcp-rs-redshift is the dilatation that carries the hidden
brane onto the visible one. Of the $15$ isometries of $AdS_5$, the dimension of the conformal group of four-dimensional
Minkowski space, the branes keep the $10$ that fix $w$, the Poincaré group of the brane world.
:::

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The same construction with other signs gives the spaces met earlier in the book. The third example compares the three
quadrics, whose curvatures differ only by the sign $N \cdot N$ in the Gauss equation.

::: {#exm-vcp-adsq-three-quadrics}
#### Sphere, de Sitter and anti-de Sitter

The sphere $\sum_i(Y^i)^2 = a^2$ in Euclidean space has $N \cdot N = 1$ and $h = \gamma/a$ for its positive-definite metric
$\gamma$, so its curvature is $+a^{-2}$, as for the $S^7$ of @exm-vcr-frg-s7. De Sitter space is the quadric $X \cdot X = -L^2$ in
Minkowski space with one time (@exm-gr-ds-hyperboloid); its normal has $N \cdot N = -1$, so $R_{\mu\nu} = -(D -
1)L^{-2}g_{\mu\nu}$ and $\Lambda = +(D - 1)(D - 2)/(2L^2)$ [@boskoff2024journey, Sec. 11.2]. Anti-de Sitter space has a
timelike normal in a space with two times, $N \cdot N = +1$, and the opposite sign. The Freund-Rubin vacuum $AdS_4 \times
S^7$ is the product of two such quadrics (@exm-vcr-frg-quadric), and the flux minimum of @exm-vcp-fluxmin-ads, with
$V(R_{\min}) < 0$, is an $AdS_4$ of the same kind.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The Poincaré coordinates are given by explicit formulas, and the check that they lie on the quadric and induce the
warped metric is mechanical. The first exercise does it with Sage for $D = 5$.

::: {#exr-vcp-adsq-poincare}
#### Poincaré coordinates with Sage

With Sage, check that the map (v) of @prp-vcp-ads-quadric for $D = 5$ lands on the quadric, pull back the flat metric,
and substitute $L = 1/k$, $w = e^{ky}/k$ to recover the Randall-Sundrum metric.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The constraint holds identically, since $(X^0)^2 - \sum_{i=1}^{3}(X^i)^2 = L^2\eta_{\mu\nu}x^\mu x^\nu/w^2$ and $(X^5)^2 -
(X^4)^2 = (X^5 + X^4)(X^5 - X^4) = L^2 - L^2\eta_{\mu\nu}x^\mu x^\nu/w^2$. The induced metric is $L^2w^{-2}(\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu
dx^\nu - dw^2)$, and with $w = e^{ky}/k$ both $L^2/w^2 = e^{-2ky}$ and $(L/w)^2(dw/dy)^2 = 1$:

{{< sage exr-vcp-adsq-poincare >}}
:::

The cosmological constant follows from the Ricci tensor by taking a trace. The second exercise derives
@eq-vcp-ads-lambda and evaluates it for the anti-de Sitter spaces of this part of the book.

::: {#exr-vcp-adsq-lambda}
#### The cosmological constant in $D$ dimensions

Take the trace of $R_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12Rg_{\mu\nu} = \Lambda g_{\mu\nu}$ in $D$ dimensions to express $R_{\mu\nu}$ through
$\Lambda$, and combine it with @eq-vcp-ads-curvature to prove @eq-vcp-ads-lambda. Evaluate $\Lambda$ for $AdS_4$ with $L =
1/2m$, for $AdS_5$ with $L = 1/k$, and for $AdS_7$ and $AdS_3$ of radius $L$ [@boskoff2024journey, Sec. 12.5].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The trace gives $R(1 - D/2) = D\Lambda$, so $R = -2D\Lambda/(D - 2)$ and $R_{\mu\nu} = (\Lambda + \tfrac12R)g_{\mu\nu} = -2\Lambda
g_{\mu\nu}/(D - 2)$. Equating with $(D - 1)L^{-2}g_{\mu\nu}$ gives @eq-vcp-ads-lambda. For $AdS_4$, $\Lambda = -3/L^2 = -12m^2$,
as in @exr-vcr-sc-lambda; for $AdS_5$, $\Lambda = -6k^2$, @eq-vcp-rs-lambda; for $AdS_7$, $\Lambda = -15/L^2$; for $AdS_3$,
$\Lambda = -1/L^2$. For $D = 2$ the Einstein tensor vanishes identically and $\Lambda = 0$ is forced, whatever $L$: two-dimensional
gravity has no Einstein equations.
:::

The dilatation of @exm-vcp-adsq-dilatation has a Killing vector that can be written down directly in the coordinates of
@eq-vcp-rs-metric. The third exercise finds it and asks what the branes do to it.

::: {#exr-vcp-adsq-killing}
#### The dilatation Killing vector

Show that the flow $y \mapsto y + s/k$, $x^\mu \mapsto e^sx^\mu$ preserves $e^{-2ky}\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - dy^2$ on $y > 0$,
write its generator $\xi$, and check $\mathcal{L}_\xi g = 0$ from the components. Is $\xi$ a symmetry of the
Randall-Sundrum model with two branes?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Under the flow $e^{-2k(y + s/k)}e^{2s}\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu = e^{-2ky}\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu$ and $dy$ is unchanged. The
generator is $\xi = x^\mu\partial_\mu + k^{-1}\partial_y$. In components, $(\mathcal{L}_\xi g)_{\mu\nu} = \xi^y\partial_yg_{\mu\nu} +
g_{\rho\nu}\partial_\mu\xi^\rho + g_{\mu\rho}\partial_\nu\xi^\rho = (-2 + 1 + 1)e^{-2ky}\eta_{\mu\nu} = 0$, and the components with a $y$
index vanish because $\xi^y$ is constant and $\xi^\mu$ does not depend on $y$. The flow moves the branes at $y = 0$ and $y =
\pi r_c$, so it is not a symmetry of the model; it maps a solution with branes at $0$ and $\pi r_c$ to one with branes at $s/k$
and $\pi r_c + s/k$, which is why only the distance $\pi r_c$, the radion, is physical (@exm-vcp-rssol-tuning).
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Flat slices are not the only possibility: the planes $X^D = \mathrm{const}$ cut the quadric in de Sitter spaces. The
fourth exercise writes anti-de Sitter space as a warped product over de Sitter slices, the geometry of a brane whose
world-volume inflates.

::: {#exr-vcp-adsq-ds-slicing}
#### De Sitter slices with Sage

Put $X^D = L\cosh(y/L)$ and $(X^0, X^1, \dots, X^{D-1}) = L\sinh(y/L)\,Y$ with $Y$ on the unit de Sitter quadric of
@exm-gr-ds-hyperboloid, and show that @eq-vcp-ads-quadric holds and that the induced metric is $\sinh^2(y/L)\,L^2ds^2_{dS} -
dy^2$ with $ds^2_{dS}$ the unit de Sitter metric. With Sage, for $D = 5$ and $ds^2_{dS} = d\tau^2 - e^{2\tau}d\vec x^2$, check
$R_{MN} = 4L^{-2}g_{MN}$ and find the Hubble rate of the slice $y = y_0$ [@boskoff2024journey, Secs. 11.4 and 12.5].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
With $Y \cdot Y = -1$, $X \cdot X = L^2\cosh^2(y/L) - L^2\sinh^2(y/L) = L^2$. Since $Y \cdot dY = 0$, the induced metric is
$\sinh^2(y/L)\,dy^2 - \cosh^2(y/L)\,dy^2 + L^2\sinh^2(y/L)\,dY \cdot dY = -dy^2 + L^2\sinh^2(y/L)\,ds^2_{dS}$. The curvature is the
anti-de Sitter one, and the slice at $y_0$ is de Sitter space with $H = 1/(L\sinh(y_0/L))$:

{{< sage exr-vcp-adsq-ds-slicing >}}

A brane placed at $y_0$ in this slicing has a world-volume that expands exponentially; as $y_0$ grows, $H \to 0$ and the
slicing approaches the flat one of the Randall-Sundrum solution, in which the tension relations of @prp-vcp-rs-solution make
the brane flat. A tension above the critical value gives a de Sitter brane, another way to think of the uplift of
@exm-vcp-fluxmin-uplift.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

Einstein metrics also solve gravitational theories other than Einstein's. The last exercise, adapted from Boskoff and
Capozziello, shows that four dimensions is special for an action quadratic in the curvature.

::: {#exr-vcp-adsq-quadratic}
#### Quadratic gravity

For an action $\int d^Dx\sqrt{|g|}\,f(R)$ the field equations are $f'(R)R_{\mu\nu} - \tfrac12f(R)g_{\mu\nu} + (g_{\mu\nu}\Box -
\nabla_\mu\nabla_\nu)f'(R) = 0$. Show that an Einstein metric $R_{\mu\nu} = (R/D)g_{\mu\nu}$ with constant $R \neq 0$, such as
@eq-vcp-ads-curvature, solves them for $f = R^2$ exactly when $D = 4$, and find the constant $\mu$ for which it solves them with
$f = R^2 - \mu$ in other dimensions [@boskoff2024journey, Sec. 11.4, Example 11.4.1].
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
For constant $R$ the derivative terms vanish. With $f = R^2 - \mu$, $f' = 2R$, the equation becomes $(2R^2/D - \tfrac12(R^2 -
\mu))g_{\mu\nu} = 0$, so $\mu = R^2(D - 4)/D$. For $f = R^2$ ($\mu = 0$) this requires $D = 4$: then $AdS_4$ and de Sitter space of
every radius are solutions, because $\int d^4x\sqrt{|g|}R^2$ is unchanged by a constant rescaling of the metric and no
length scale is selected. For $AdS_5$, $R = 20/L^2$ and $\mu = 80/L^4$; the radius is then fixed by $\mu$, as $L$ is fixed by
$\Lambda$ in Einstein gravity.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The warped metric solves the five-dimensional Einstein equations with a negative cosmological constant in the bulk
and tensions on the branes. The proposition derives this from the Einstein tensor of a general warp function.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-vcp-rs-solution}
#### The warped solution

Take the action $S = -\frac{1}{2\kappa_5^2}\int d^5x\sqrt{|g|}\,(R + 2\Lambda) - \sum_iV_i\int_{y = y_i}d^4x\sqrt{|g_4|}$, the
convention of @def-cosmological-constant with brane tensions $V_i$, so that $G_{MN} - \Lambda g_{MN} = \kappa_5^2T_{MN}$
with $T_{\mu\nu} = V_i\delta(y - y_i)g_{\mu\nu}$ on the branes. For $ds^2 = e^{-2A(y)}\eta_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - dy^2$,
$$
G_{\mu\nu} = \left(3A'' - 6A'^2\right)g_{\mu\nu}, \qquad G_{yy} = -6A'^2g_{yy}, \qquad G_{\mu y} = 0 .
$$ {#eq-vcp-warped-einstein}
In the bulk the equations force $A'^2 = -\Lambda/6$ and $A'' = 0$, solved by $A = k|y|$ with
$$
\Lambda = -6k^2 ;
$$ {#eq-vcp-rs-lambda}
the kinks $A'' = 2k\delta(y) - 2k\delta(y - \pi r_c)$ require the tensions $V_0 = -V_\pi = 6k/\kappa_5^2$. In the normalisation of
@randall1999a, $\frac{1}{2\kappa_5^2} = 2M^3$ and $\Lambda_{\rm RS} = \Lambda/\kappa_5^2$, these read $k^2 = -\Lambda_{\rm RS}/(24M^3)$ and
$V_0 = -V_\pi = 24M^3k$ [@randall1999a, eqs. 7-11]. The four-dimensional Planck mass is
$$
M_{\rm Pl}^2 = M^3r_c\int_{-\pi}^{\pi}e^{-2kr_c|\phi|}d\phi = \frac{M^3}{k}\left(1 - e^{-2kr_c\pi}\right)
$$ {#eq-vcp-rs-planck}
[@randall1999a, eq. 16], finite as $r_c \to \infty$.
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

curvature conventions of the book, the bulk equations for $A = \pm ky$, the tension, the conversion to the normalisation

![The Randall-Sundrum geometry. Left: the warp factor $e^{-2k|y|}$ for $k = 0.5, 1, 2$, peaked at the brane $y = 0$.
Right: in the conformal coordinate $z$, the normalised graviton zero mode $\sqrt k\,(k|z| + 1)^{-3/2}$ (solid) and the
potential $15k^2/(8(k|z| + 1)^2)$ of the analogue Schrödinger problem, scaled by $\tfrac14$ (dashed; the attractive
$-\tfrac32k\delta(z)$ at the brane is not drawn). Generated by `figures/warp_factor.sage`.](figures/warp_factor.svg){#fig-warp-factor width=95%}

{{< interactive warp_factor 460 >}}

The visible brane of the original model sits at $y = \pi r_c$. Everything on it is red-shifted, and a modest $kr_c$
produces the electroweak scale from the Planck scale.

::: {#exm-vcp-rssol-hierarchy}
#### The hierarchy

A Higgs field on the brane at $y = \pi r_c$ with vacuum value $v_0$ in the brane action has, after the field is rescaled
to a canonical kinetic term, the vacuum value $v = e^{-kr_c\pi}v_0$, and every mass parameter is reduced by the same
factor, $m = e^{-kr_c\pi}m_0$ [@randall1999a, eqs. 17-21]. A factor $10^{-15}$ needs only
$kr_c = 15\log 10/\pi \approx 11$ (the arXiv text of @randall1999a prints $kr_c \approx 50$ here, which would give
$e^{-50\pi} \approx 10^{-68}$): an exponential hierarchy from a radius only ten times the curvature length.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** The rescaling of the mass parameters is checked in `figures/warp_factor.sage`.
:::

The Planck mass @eq-vcp-rs-planck depends on $r_c$ only through an exponentially small term. The second brane can
therefore be removed without changing four-dimensional gravity.

::: {#exm-vcp-rssol-planck}
#### Gravity with an infinite dimension

As $r_c \to \infty$, $M_{\rm Pl}^2 \to M^3/k$: "there is a well-defined value for $M_{\rm Pl}$, even in the $r_c \to \infty$
limit", in contrast to the product-space expectation $M_{\rm Pl}^2 = M^3r_c\pi$ [@randall1999b, eq. 7]. The four-dimensional
Planck mass is fixed by the curvature $k$ of the bulk, not by its size.
:::

The solution exists only for special values of the tensions. The tuning is the cosmological constant problem in
another guise, and the radius is left undetermined.

::: {#exm-vcp-rssol-tuning}
#### Tuning and the radion

The relations $V_0 = -V_\pi = 6k/\kappa_5^2$, $\Lambda = -6k^2$ are needed for flat branes; they amount to setting the
four-dimensional cosmological constant to zero, "a necessary fine tuning" [@randall1999b, eq. 5]. The radius $r_c$ is an
integration constant of the solution [@randall1999a, Sec. 3], a modulus (@def-vcp-modulus), the radion, which must be
given a potential by some other mechanism.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The hierarchy depends exponentially on $kr_c$, so small changes of $kr_c$ have large effects. The first exercise
tabulates the values needed.

::: {#exr-vcp-rssol-scales}
#### How large is $kr_c$, with Sage

Compute $kr_c = \log(m_0/m)/\pi$ for $(m_0, m) = (10^{15}, 1)$, $(10^{18}, 246)$ and $(2.4 \times 10^{18}, 10^3)$ in GeV with
Sage, the correction $e^{-2kr_c\pi}$ in @eq-vcp-rs-planck, and the change of $m$ when $kr_c$ grows by $10\%$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$kr_c \approx 11.0$, $11.4$ and $11.3$; the correction to $M_{\rm Pl}$ is below $10^{-30}$; a $10\%$ change of $kr_c$ changes $m$
by a factor $e^{-0.1kr_c\pi} \approx 0.03$. The radius must therefore be stabilised with some precision, the role of the
radion potential:

{{< sage exr-vcp-rssol-scales >}}
:::

The red-shift of the Higgs vacuum value can be followed step by step through the brane action. The second exercise
asks for the steps.

::: {#exr-vcp-rssol-higgs}
#### The warped Higgs

The visible-brane action is $\int d^4x\sqrt{|g_{\rm vis}|}\{g_{\rm vis}^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu H^\dagger\partial_\nu H - \lambda(|H|^2 -
v_0^2)^2\}$ with $g^{\rm vis}_{\mu\nu} = e^{-2kr_c\pi}\eta_{\mu\nu}$. Show that after $H \to e^{kr_c\pi}H$ it becomes the standard
Higgs action with $v_0$ replaced by $e^{-kr_c\pi}v_0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sqrt{|g_{\rm vis}|} = e^{-4kr_c\pi}$ and $g_{\rm vis}^{\mu\nu} = e^{2kr_c\pi}\eta^{\mu\nu}$, so the action is $\int e^{-4kr_c\pi}\{e^{2kr_c\pi} |
\partial H|^2 - \lambda(|H|^2 - v_0^2)^2\}$. With $H = e^{kr_c\pi}\tilde H$ the kinetic term becomes $|\partial\tilde H|^2$ and the
potential $e^{-4kr_c\pi}\lambda(e^{2kr_c\pi}|\tilde H|^2 - v_0^2)^2 = \lambda(|\tilde H|^2 - e^{-2kr_c\pi}v_0^2)^2$: the vacuum value is
$e^{-kr_c\pi}v_0$ [@randall1999a, eqs. 17-20].
:::

The relation between $M_{\rm Pl}$ and the five-dimensional parameters depends on how the four-dimensional action is
normalised. The third exercise tracks the factors.

::: {#exr-vcp-rssol-normalisation}
#### Normalisation of the Planck mass

With the five-dimensional action $2M^3\int\sqrt{|g|}R$ and $ds^2 = e^{-2k|y|}\bar g_{\mu\nu}dx^\mu dx^\nu - dy^2$, the
four-dimensional curvature term is $2M^3\int dy\,e^{-2k|y|}\int\sqrt{|\bar g|}\bar R$. Find $M_{\rm Pl}^2$ if the
four-dimensional action is written $2M_{\rm Pl}^2\int\sqrt{|\bar g|}\bar R$, and if it is written $\tfrac12M_{\rm Pl}^2\int
\sqrt{|\bar g|}\bar R$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$\sqrt{|g_5|}R_5 \supset e^{-4k|y|}e^{2k|y|}\sqrt{|\bar g|}\bar R$, so the coefficient is $2M^3\int_{-\pi r_c}^{\pi r_c}e^{-2k|y|}dy =
\frac{2M^3}{k}(1 - e^{-2kr_c\pi})$. Matching to $2M_{\rm Pl}^2$ gives @eq-vcp-rs-planck; matching to $\tfrac12M_{\rm Pl}^2$ gives four
times as much. The exponential dependence on $kr_c$, which is what matters, is the same in both conventions.
:::
::::

### The localised graviton

In a product compactification the massless graviton has a constant profile over the internal space. In the warped
geometry its profile follows the warp factor, and it is concentrated near the positive-tension brane even when the
fifth dimension is infinite.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcp-graviton-zero-mode}
#### Graviton zero mode

Perturb @eq-vcp-rs-metric to $g_{\mu\nu} = e^{-2k|y|}\eta_{\mu\nu} + h_{\mu\nu}(x, y)$ with $h_{\mu\nu} = \psi(y)\epsilon_{\mu\nu}
e^{ip\cdot x}$, $p^2 = m^2$, in the gauge $\partial^\mu h_{\mu\nu} = h^\mu{}_\mu = 0$. The linearised Einstein equations give
$\left[-\tfrac{m^2}{2}e^{2k|y|} - \tfrac12\partial_y^2 - 2k\delta(y) + 2k^2\right]\psi = 0$ [@randall1999b, eq. 8]; in the
variables $z = \operatorname{sgn}(y)(e^{k|y|} - 1)/k$, $\hat\psi = \psi e^{k|y|/2}$ this is a Schrödinger problem with the
"volcano" potential
$$
V(z) = \frac{15k^2}{8(k|z| + 1)^2} - \frac{3k}{2}\delta(z)
$$ {#eq-vcp-volcano}
[@randall1999b, eqs. 9-10]. The **graviton zero mode** is its $m = 0$ solution,
$$
\psi_0 = e^{-2k|y|}, \qquad \hat\psi_0(z) = \sqrt k\,(k|z| + 1)^{-3/2} ,
$$ {#eq-vcp-zero-mode}
normalisable on the whole line: the four-dimensional graviton. The modes with $m > 0$ form a continuum with no gap,
suppressed near $z = 0$ by the barrier of the potential [@randall1999b, p. 4].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The zero mode is concentrated within a distance $1/k$ of the brane. The fraction of its norm there is a simple
integral.

::: {#exm-vcp-zero-localised}
#### Localisation

$\int|\hat\psi_0|^2dz = 2\int_0^\infty k(kz + 1)^{-3}dz = 1$, and the fraction within $|z| < n/k$ is $1 - (n + 1)^{-2}$: $\tfrac34$ within
one curvature length, $99\%$ within $|z| < 9/k$ (@exr-vcp-zero-norm, @fig-warp-factor). Although space is infinite in
extent, "the graviton is confined to a small region within this space" [@randall1999b, p. 2].
:::

The continuum of massive modes modifies Newton's law at short distances. The correction is suppressed by the
curvature length. It is computed in @exr-vcp-zero-newton.

::: {#exm-vcp-zero-newton}
#### Newton's law on the brane

Exchange of the zero mode gives $G_Nm_1m_2/r$; the continuum of massive gravitons, each giving a Yukawa potential with
coupling suppressed by $m/k$, adds a correction, and $V(r) = \frac{G_Nm_1m_2}{r}\left(1 + \frac{1}{r^2k^2}\right)$ [@randall1999b,
eqs. 15-16] (@exr-vcp-zero-newton). For $k$ of order the Planck scale the correction is unobservable at any distance
tested.
:::

With two branes the spectrum is discrete. The masses are set by the red-shifted scale of the visible brane, not by
$1/r_c$.

::: {#exm-vcp-zero-two-branes}
#### Kaluza-Klein gravitons at the TeV scale

With the second brane at $y = \pi r_c$ the continuum becomes a discrete tower with spacing of order $ke^{-kr_c\pi}$, the TeV
scale for $kr_c \approx 11$: "there are no light Kaluza-Klein modes", and each excitation couples to matter on the visible
brane with TeV-scale strength [@randall1999a, Sec. 1], $10^{15}$ times more strongly than the massless graviton
[@randall1999b, p. 6].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The normalisation and the localisation fractions are elementary integrals. The first exercise computes them with
Sage. They also confirm that the zero mode solves the equation with the delta function.

::: {#exr-vcp-zero-norm}
#### Normalisation with Sage

Show with Sage that $\hat\psi_0 = \sqrt k(k|z| + 1)^{-3/2}$ has unit norm and that the probability of $|z| < n/k$ is $1 - 1/(n +
1)^2$. Check also that $\hat\psi_0$ solves the Schrödinger equation with the potential @eq-vcp-volcano at $m = 0$, including
the jump at $z = 0$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The norm is $1$ and the probabilities for $n = 1, 2, 10$ are $\tfrac34$, $\tfrac89$, $\tfrac{120}{121}$:

{{< sage exr-vcp-zero-norm >}}

For $z > 0$, $\hat\psi_0'' = \tfrac{15}{4}k^2(kz + 1)^{-2}\hat\psi_0$, so $-\tfrac12\hat\psi_0'' + \tfrac{15k^2}{8(kz + 1)^2}\hat\psi_0 =
0$; and $\hat\psi_0'(0^+) - \hat\psi_0'(0^-) = -3k\hat\psi_0(0)$, which is what integrating $-\tfrac12\hat\psi'' - \tfrac32k\delta(z)\hat\psi
= 0$ across $z = 0$ requires (checked in `warp_factor.sage`).
:::

The correction to Newton's law is a superposition of Yukawa potentials. The second exercise performs the
superposition. Each massive graviton contributes a Yukawa term.

::: {#exr-vcp-zero-newton}
#### The Newtonian correction with Sage

Integrate $\int_0^\infty dm\,\frac{G_N}{k}\frac mk\frac{e^{-mr}}{r}$ with Sage and evaluate the relative correction $1/(kr)^2$ for
$1/k$ equal to the Planck length and to $0.1$ mm, at $r = 1$ mm.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The integral is $G_N/(k^2r^3)$, giving @randall1999b's correction. For $1/k = 1.6 \times 10^{-35}$ m it is $10^{-64}$ at a
millimetre; for $1/k = 0.1$ mm it would be $1\%$, so tests of Newton's law below a millimetre bound the curvature
length:

{{< sage exr-vcp-zero-newton >}}
:::

A flat extra dimension also has a constant zero mode, but its normalisation grows with the size. The third exercise
compares the two cases.

::: {#exr-vcp-zero-flat}
#### Flat versus warped

For a flat extra dimension of length $L$ the graviton zero mode is constant. Find its normalised profile and the
four-dimensional Planck mass as functions of $L$, and explain why $L \to \infty$ gives five-dimensional gravity while $r_c
\to \infty$ in the warped case does not.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The normalised constant mode is $1/\sqrt L$ and $M_{\rm Pl}^2 \propto M^3L$, so the coupling of the zero mode, $1/M_{\rm Pl}$,
vanishes as $L \to \infty$, while the massive modes $n/L$ become a continuum that couples unsuppressed: gravity becomes
five-dimensional. In the warped case the zero mode has finite norm with $L$ infinite, $M_{\rm Pl}^2 \to M^3/k$, and the
continuum is suppressed near the brane by the volcano barrier, so the zero mode dominates at distances $r \gg 1/k$.
:::
::::

### Large extra dimensions

If gravity alone propagates in the extra dimensions, they can be much larger than the distances at which the other
forces have been tested. The four-dimensional Planck mass then measures the volume of the extra space.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-vcp-large-extra-dimensions}
#### Large extra dimensions

In the scenario of **large extra dimensions** spacetime is $\mathbb{R}^4 \times M_n$, $n \ge 2$, with $M_n$ compact of
volume $R^n$; the Standard Model fields are confined to a four-dimensional submanifold of thickness about $1/M$, and only
gravity, with fundamental scale $M$, propagates in the bulk. Gauss's law in $4 + n$ dimensions gives the potential
$V(r) \sim \frac{m_1m_2}{M^{n+2}r^{n+1}}$ for $r \ll R$ and $\frac{m_1m_2}{M^{n+2}R^nr}$ for $r \gg R$, hence
$$
M_{\rm Pl}^2 \sim M^{n+2}R^n
$$ {#eq-vcp-add-planck}
[@arkanihamed1998, eqs. 1-3]. In four-dimensional language the bulk graviton is a tower of Kaluza-Klein gravitons
"recurring once every $1/R$" in mass, each coupled with strength $1/M_{\rm Pl}$ [@arkanihamed1998, Sec. 2].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
With $M$ at the TeV scale the size follows from @eq-vcp-add-planck. One extra dimension would have to be as large as
the solar system.

::: {#exm-vcp-add-sizes}
#### How large

With $M = 1$ TeV and $M_{\rm Pl} = G_N^{-1/2} = 1.22 \times 10^{19}$ GeV, $R = (M_{\rm Pl}^2/M^{n+2})^{1/n}$ is $3 \times 10^{13}$ m
for $n = 1$, excluded by planetary motion, and $2.4$ mm for $n = 2$, at the edge of the tests of Newton's law
(@prp-vcp-add-planck); @arkanihamed1998 [eq. 4] quote $10^{13}$ cm and $0.1$-$1$ mm with $M_{\rm Pl} \sim 10^{18}$ GeV.
:::

For a torus the relation @eq-vcp-add-planck is exact up to factors of $2\pi$. It is the Kaluza-Klein reduction of the
Einstein-Hilbert action, as in Part III.

::: {#exm-vcp-add-torus}
#### Reduction on a torus

Reducing the $(4 + n)$-dimensional Einstein-Hilbert action $M^{n+2}\int\sqrt{|g|}R$ on a torus of radius $R_t$, with fields
independent of the extra coordinates, multiplies it by the volume $(2\pi R_t)^n$: $M_{\rm Pl}^2 = M^{n+2}(2\pi R_t)^n$
[@douglas2006, Sec. II.A, eq. 1]. For $n = 1$ this is the relation between the Planck length, the radius and the
five-dimensional coupling of @def-planck-radius-relation.
:::

The gauge forces have been tested at distances far below a millimetre. The fields that carry them must therefore be
confined, which is the role of the brane.

::: {#exm-vcp-add-brane}
#### Why the Standard Model lives on a brane

"The SM particles cannot freely propagate in the extra $n$ dimension, but must be localized to a 4 dimensional
submanifold" because gauge forces are measured accurately at weak-scale distances [@arkanihamed1998, Sec. 1]. Gravity is
measured only down to about a millimetre, so it alone can feel the large dimensions. D-branes in string theory provide
such submanifolds naturally [@arkanihamed1998, Sec. 1].
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The first exercise tabulates the sizes. It also shows how much the $2\pi$ of the torus convention changes them. The numbers are those of @fig-add-planck.

::: {#exr-vcp-add-table}
#### Sizes with Sage

Tabulate with Sage, for $n = 1, \dots, 7$ and $M = 1$ TeV, the size $R$ from @eq-vcp-add-planck, the spacing $1/R$ of the
Kaluza-Klein gravitons in eV, and the torus radius $R_t = R/2\pi$ of @exm-vcp-add-torus.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$R$ falls from $3 \times 10^{13}$ m ($n = 1$) and $2.4$ mm ($n = 2$) to about $10^{-14}$ m for $n = 6, 7$, where $1/R$ is in the
MeV range; for $n = 2$, $1/R \approx 10^{-4}$ eV, so the tower is practically continuous at collider energies:

{{< sage exr-vcp-add-table >}}
:::

The number of gravitons light enough to be produced grows as a power of the energy. The second exercise counts them
on a torus.

::: {#exr-vcp-add-kkcount}
#### Counting Kaluza-Klein gravitons with Sage

The Kaluza-Klein gravitons on a torus of radius $R_t$ have masses $|k|/R_t$, $k \in \mathbb{Z}^n$. Count with Sage those below
$E$ for $n = 1, 2, 3$ and $ER_t = 5, 10, 20$, and compare with $\Omega_n(ER_t)^n$, $\Omega_n$ the volume of the unit ball.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The counts approach $\Omega_n(ER_t)^n$ within a few per cent, the multiplicity $(ER)^n$ of @arkanihamed1998 [Sec. 2] up to
the constant $\Omega_n$:

{{< sage exr-vcp-add-kkcount >}}
:::

Gauss's law fixes the force law on both sides of the crossover. The third exercise looks at the short-distance side,
where the deviation from Newton's law would be seen.

::: {#exr-vcp-add-crossover}
#### The force at short distances

For $n = 2$ and $r \ll R$, how does the gravitational force between two masses depend on $r$? By what factor does it exceed
the Newtonian force at $r = R/10$, assuming the two expressions of @def-vcp-large-extra-dimensions match at $r = R$?
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$V \propto 1/r^3$ gives $F \propto 1/r^4$ instead of $1/r^2$ [@arkanihamed1998, Sec. 2]. Matching at $r = R$, $F(r)/F_{\rm
Newton}(r) = (R/r)^2$, which is $100$ at $r = R/10$: a millimetre-sized $R$ would show up as a strong enhancement of
gravity in sub-millimetre torsion-balance experiments.
:::
::::

The relation between the Planck mass and the size of large extra dimensions, and the graviton multiplicities it
implies, reduce to algebra and arithmetic. The proposition records them.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-vcp-add-planck}
#### Planck mass from large extra dimensions

The potentials $\frac{m_1m_2}{M^{n+2}r^{n+1}}$ and $\frac{m_1m_2}{M^{n+2}R^nr}$ agree at $r = R$, and matching the second to
$\frac{m_1m_2}{M_{\rm Pl}^2r}$ gives $M_{\rm Pl}^2 = M^{n+2}R^n$. With $M_{\rm Pl} = 1.22 \times 10^{19}$ GeV and $M = 1$ TeV, $R = 2.9 \times
10^{13}$ m for $n = 1$, $2.4$ mm for $n = 2$ and $4.5 \times 10^{-14}$ m for $n = 6$, decreasing with $n$ and with $M$; the
Kaluza-Klein spacing for $n = 2$ is $8 \times 10^{-5}$ eV; and the summed graviton emission rate satisfies $(ER)^n/M_{\rm Pl}^2
= E^n/M^{n+2}$.
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Checked by exact computation in `figures/add_planck.sage`, with the Kaluza-Klein mode count on a torus against the
volume of a ball.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
![Large extra dimensions: $\log_{10}$ of the size $R$ (in metres) of $n$ extra dimensions for a fundamental scale $M = 1$ TeV
(red) and $10$ TeV (blue), from $M_{\rm Pl}^2 = M^{n+2}R^n$. The dashed line is $0.1$ mm, the scale of laboratory tests of
Newton's law; the dotted line is the size of the solar system. Generated by
`figures/add_planck.sage`.](figures/add_planck.svg){#fig-add-planck width=70%}

{{< interactive add_planck 460 >}}

Individually each graviton couples with $1/M_{\rm Pl}$, but there are many of them. Their combined emission rate is
suppressed only by the fundamental scale.

::: {#exm-vcp-add-emission}
#### Graviton emission at colliders

The number of gravitons below $E$ is about $(ER)^n$, so the total rate of emission is $(ER)^n/M_{\rm Pl}^2 = E^n/M^{n+2}$
[@arkanihamed1998, eqs. 5-6]: at $E \sim M \sim 1$ TeV gravity is as strong as the other interactions, with missing-energy
signatures at colliders.
:::

Stars emit gravitons too. The hottest astrophysical environments give the strongest bounds for $n = 2$. Gravitons carry energy away from the core.

::: {#exm-vcp-add-supernova}
#### Supernova cooling

In the core of a supernova, $E \approx 20$ MeV, and the branching ratio $(E/M)^{n+2}$ for $M = 1$ TeV and $n = 2$ is $1.6 \times
10^{-19}$ (@exr-vcp-add-emission). Graviton emission from SN 1987A constrains $n = 2$ with $M = 1$ TeV and is
"easily satisfied if $n > 2$ or if $m_{EW} > 10$ TeV" [@arkanihamed1998, Sec. 2].
:::

The two proposals of this section explain the same hierarchy in different ways. Comparing them shows what each
assumes. Both trade the hierarchy for a property of the extra dimensions.

::: {#exm-vcp-add-vs-rs}
#### Large versus warped

In large extra dimensions $M_{\rm Pl}/M$ is a power of $MR$, so $R$ must be large: $(M_{\rm Pl}/M)^{2/n}$ in units of $1/M$. In the
warped model it is an exponential of $kr_c$, and $kr_c \approx 11$ suffices; there is "one additional dimension, as opposed to
$n \ge 2$", and no light Kaluza-Klein modes [@randall1999a, Sec. 1]. In both the size of the extra dimension is a modulus
that must be stabilised.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The identity behind @exm-vcp-add-emission is a one-line consequence of @eq-vcp-add-planck. The first exercise checks it and
evaluates branching ratios. The numbers show where the effect is large and where it is negligible.

::: {#exr-vcp-add-emission}
#### Emission rates with Sage

Verify $(ER)^n/(M^{n+2}R^n) = E^n/M^{n+2}$ with Sage and evaluate $(E/M)^{n+2}$ for $M = 1$ TeV, $n = 2, 3, 6$ and $E = 20$ MeV,
$100$ GeV, $1$ TeV.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
The identity holds for all $n$; the branching ratios range from $10^{-19}$ ($n = 2$) and $10^{-38}$ ($n = 6$) in a
supernova to order one at $E = M$:

{{< sage exr-vcp-add-emission >}}
:::

Large extra dimensions replace the question "why is $M_{\rm Pl}$ large?" by another. The second exercise identifies it. The answer concerns the modulus of the scenario.

::: {#exr-vcp-add-question}
#### What is left unexplained

Express $MR$ for $n = 2$ and $M = 1$ TeV as a pure number, and explain why the scenario still needs a mechanism for the size
of the extra dimensions. Compare with the role of $kr_c$ in @exm-vcp-rssol-tuning.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$R = 2.4$ mm $= 1.2 \times 10^{13}$ GeV$^{-1}$, so $MR \approx 10^{16}$: the large number reappears as the size of the extra
dimensions in fundamental units. @arkanihamed1998 [Sec. 4] stress that $R$ is "a parameter characterizing a solution"
rather than a Lagrangian parameter, so no symmetry is needed to keep it large, but why it takes this value is "not
addressed": the radius is a modulus (@def-vcp-modulus) whose potential must have its minimum there. In the warped case
$kr_c \approx 11$ is a modest number, which is the main appeal of that proposal.
:::

The Kaluza-Klein gravitons of large extra dimensions are almost massless and extremely weakly coupled individually.
The third exercise contrasts them with the Kaluza-Klein modes of Part III.

::: {#exr-vcp-add-compare-kk}
#### Kaluza-Klein modes then and now

In Part III the circle radius is of order the Planck length (@def-planck-radius-relation) and all charged matter
propagates in five dimensions. Compare the mass of the first Kaluza-Klein mode and its coupling with those of the first
Kaluza-Klein graviton for $n = 2$, $M = 1$ TeV.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
In Part III $m_1 = 1/R \sim M_{\rm Pl}/80 \approx 10^{17}$ GeV, far beyond any experiment, and the modes carry charge
(@def-charge-quantisation). For large extra dimensions $m_1 \approx 10^{-4}$ eV (@exr-vcp-add-table), so millions of
gravitons are produced in a collision at a GeV, each with coupling $1/M_{\rm Pl}$, invisible singly but significant
in sum (@exm-vcp-add-emission). The Standard Model fields have no tower at all, being confined to the brane.
:::
::::

## Fermions on compact spaces {#sec-compactification-fermions}

The compactifications of this chapter were chosen for what they leave at low energies, and the most important of these
leftovers are chiral fermions. Their number was quoted in @prp-vcp-generations as half the Euler number; this section derives
it from the fermions themselves. The starting point in every case is the ten-dimensional $E_8$ gaugino, a Majorana-Weyl
spinor in the $\mathbf{248}$, and the mechanism is always the one of @sec-csdr-fermions: a background gauge field embedded in a
subgroup of $E_8$ that commutes with $E_6$ turns the internal Dirac operator into a twisted one, whose zero modes in the
$\mathbf{27}$ are the families. On the nearly-Kähler cosets the background is fixed by the CSDR constraints and the count is a
matching of representations of the isotropy group; on Calabi-Yau spaces it is the spin connection itself and the count is a
pair of Hodge numbers; on the orbifold $T^6/\mathbb{Z}_3$ it is a projection, completed by the string at the fixed points. The
analysis of the Dirac operators, the index and the Euler number is in @sec-dirac-compact-spaces and @sec-dirac-index; here
the physics follows @manousselis2000 [Secs. 2-4] and @chatzistavrakidis2009nk [Sec. 4] for the cosets, @braun2009 [Secs. 1
and 3] for Calabi-Yau spaces, and @ramossanchez2008 [Sec. 2.2 and App. D] for the orbifold. The Einstein-Dirac system of
@zhelnorovich2019spinors [Ch. 6] shows what a classical spinor would do to the geometry.

### Coset spaces

On a coset $S/R$ the fermions that survive CSDR are those whose $R$-representation in $F$ matches one in the spinor of the
tangent space. The figure shows the matching for the flag manifold, where $R$ is a torus and representations are points in a
plane.

![The charges under the isotropy torus $U(1) \times U(1)$ of $SU(3)/(U(1) \times U(1))$, in the basis of @chatzistavrakidis2009nk [eqs.
(4.30)-(4.31)]. Squares: the tangent space, weights $\pm\beta_i$ with $\beta_1 = (1, 1)$, $\beta_2 = (-1, 1)$, $\beta_3 = (0, -2)$. Yellow: the Weyl spinor of
$SO(6)$, weights $0$ and $\beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3$. Triangles and crosses: the components of the $\mathbf{248}$ of $E_8$ under $U(1)^2 \times E_6$. The
$\mathbf{78}$ and two singlets sit at $0$ and the three $\mathbf{27}$s at the $\beta_i$, on spinor weights: one vector multiplet and three families
(@prp-cff-nk-fermions). Generated by `figures/cff-flag-weights.sage`.](figures/cff-flag-weights.svg){#fig-cff-flag-weights width=62%}

The proposition applies the fermion rule of @prp-csf-fermion-constraint, in the form of @manousselis2000 [eqs. (12)-(15)], to the
three cosets of @def-vcp-nearly-kahler. The ten-dimensional theory is $\mathcal N = 1$ super-Yang-Mills theory with gauge group $E_8$, whose
fermion is in the adjoint.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#prp-cff-nk-fermions}
#### Fermions of $E_8$ over the nearly-Kähler cosets

Reduce ten-dimensional $E_8$ super-Yang-Mills theory, with a Majorana-Weyl gaugino in the $\mathbf{248}$, over $S/R$ by CSDR with $R$ embedded in
$E_8$ so that $H = C_{E_8}(R) \supset E_6$. The four-dimensional fermions are the components of the $\mathbf{248}$ whose $R$-representation occurs in the
Weyl spinor of $SO(6)$:

(a) $G_2/SU(3)$: the spinor is $\mathbf 1 + \mathbf 3$ of $SU(3)$ and $\mathbf{248} = (\mathbf 8, \mathbf 1) + (\mathbf 1, \mathbf{78}) + (\mathbf 3, \mathbf{27}) + (\bar{\mathbf 3},
\overline{\mathbf{27}})$, giving fermions in the $\mathbf{78}$ and one $\mathbf{27}$ of $H = E_6$;

(b) $Sp(4)/(SU(2) \times U(1))$: $H = E_6 \times U(1)$, fermions in the $\mathbf{78}$ and two $\mathbf{27}$s;

(c) $SU(3)/(U(1) \times U(1))$: the spinor has the weights $0, \beta_1, \beta_2, \beta_3$, the $\mathbf{27}$s of $\mathbf{248}$ have the weights $\beta_i$, and the
fermions are in the $\mathbf{78}$, two singlets and three $\mathbf{27}$s of $H = E_6 \times U(1)^2$.

Together with the scalars they form an $\mathcal N = 1$ vector multiplet of $E_6$ and $1$, $2$, $3$ chiral multiplets in the $\mathbf{27}$: $\tfrac12\chi(S/R)$
families [@manousselis2000, Sec. 4, eqs. (27)-(28); @chatzistavrakidis2009nk, Secs. 4.1-4.3, eqs. (4.4)-(4.5), (4.30)-(4.31)].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The six-sphere is the simplest case: the isotropy group is $SU(3)$ and the matching is a statement about $SU(3)$ representations.
The first example works it out.

::: {#exm-cff-g2su3}
#### $G_2/SU(3)$

Under $SU(3) \subset SO(6) = SU(4)/\mathbb{Z}_2$ the spinor $\mathbf 4$ is $\mathbf 1 + \mathbf 3$ and the vector $\mathbf 6$ is $\mathbf 3 + \bar{\mathbf 3}$ (@exr-spd-su3-singlets). The
singlet matches $(\mathbf 1, \mathbf{78})$: one $E_6$ gaugino. The $\mathbf 3$ matches $(\mathbf 3, \mathbf{27})$: one fermion in the $\mathbf{27}$. The vector matches $(\mathbf 3,
\mathbf{27}) + (\bar{\mathbf 3}, \overline{\mathbf{27}})$: one complex scalar in the $\mathbf{27}$. Nothing matches $(\mathbf 8, \mathbf 1)$, so the $SU(3)$ gauginos disappear
[@manousselis2000, Sec. 4]. One family, and $\chi(S^6) = 2$.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

On the flag manifold the representations are charges, and the matching can be read off @fig-cff-flag-weights. The second example
lists the result and notes a misprint in the source.

::: {#exm-cff-flag}
#### $SU(3)/(U(1) \times U(1))$

The decomposition @chatzistavrakidis2009nk [eq. (4.30)] puts the $\mathbf{27}$s at $(1, 1), (-1, 1), (0, -2)$, the $\overline{\mathbf{27}}$s at their negatives, the $\mathbf{78}$
and two singlets at $(0, 0)$ and six singlets at $(\pm1, 3)$, $(\pm2, 0)$, $(\pm1, -3)$. The spinor weights are $(0, 0), (1, 1), (-1, 1), (0, -2)$ (@exr-cff-spinor-weights;
the source prints the last as $(0, -1)$, which cannot be right since the four weights must sum to zero). The match keeps the $\mathbf{78}$, two
singlets and three $\mathbf{27}$s; the three families are labelled by the three pairs of roots of $SU(3)$, as in @exm-spd-generations-cosets.
:::

The symmetric six-sphere $SO(7)/SO(6)$ is the same manifold with a different coset structure. The third example shows that the
fermion content changes completely.

::: {#exm-cff-s6-symmetric}
#### $SO(7)/SO(6)$

With $R = SO(6)$ embedded by $E_8 \supset SO(6) \times SO(10)$, $\mathbf{248} = (\mathbf{15}, \mathbf 1) + (\mathbf 1, \mathbf{45}) + (\mathbf 6, \mathbf{10}) + (\mathbf 4, \mathbf{16}) +
(\bar{\mathbf 4}, \overline{\mathbf{16}})$, the spinor $\mathbf 4$ matches $(\mathbf 4, \mathbf{16})$ and the vector $\mathbf 6$ matches $(\mathbf 6, \mathbf{10})$: $H = SO(10)$ with
one left-handed fermion in the $\mathbf{16}$ and one scalar in the $\mathbf{10}$, and no gaugino, so no supersymmetry survives [@manousselis2000, Sec. 3,
eq. (26)]. The family is there, but the $SO(10)$ gauginos are not: the isotropy group decides which multiplets are complete.
:::

:::: {.callout-note .exercises-fold collapse="true" title="Exercises"}
The spinor weights of the flag manifold follow from those of $SO(6)$. The first exercise computes them with Sage and does the
matching.

::: {#exr-cff-spinor-weights}
#### The matching on the flag manifold

With $\beta_1 = (1, 1)$, $\beta_2 = (-1, 1)$, $\beta_3 = (0, -2)$ the holomorphic tangent weights, the Weyl spinor of $SO(6)$ has the weights $\tfrac12(\pm\beta_1
\pm\beta_2 \pm\beta_3)$ with an even number of minus signs. With Sage, compute them, match them against the decomposition of @exm-cff-flag, and count
the surviving fermions by representation of $E_6$.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Since $\beta_1 + \beta_2 + \beta_3 = 0$, $\tfrac12(\beta_1 + \beta_2 + \beta_3) = 0$ and $\tfrac12(\beta_1 - \beta_2 - \beta_3) = \beta_1$, and similarly for the other two:

{{< sage exr-cff-spinor-weights >}}

The match keeps $1 \times \mathbf{78}$, $2 \times \mathbf 1$ and $3 \times \mathbf{27}$: three families, $\tfrac12\chi = 3$ (@exr-vcp-generations-weyl).
:::

A vector multiplet and chiral multiplets have equal numbers of bosonic and fermionic states. The second exercise checks this for
the reduction over $G_2/SU(3)$.

::: {#exr-cff-multiplets}
#### Counting states

Over $G_2/SU(3)$ the four-dimensional fields are the $E_6$ gauge field, the fermions of @exm-cff-g2su3 and the complex scalars in the $\mathbf{27}$.
Count on-shell bosonic and fermionic degrees of freedom and show that they form one vector multiplet and one chiral multiplet of
$\mathcal N = 1$ (@def-supermultiplet).
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
Vector multiplet: $78 \times 2$ gauge boson states and $78 \times 2$ states of the Weyl gaugino. Chiral multiplet: $27 \times 2$ real scalar states (one
complex scalar per component) and $27 \times 2$ states of a Weyl fermion. In total $210$ bosonic and $210$ fermionic states, organised as $\mathcal N = 1$
multiplets; the reduction preserves one four-dimensional supersymmetry, up to the soft terms of @def-cff-geometric-mass and of the potential
[@manousselis2000, Sec. 4].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

The families equal half the Euler number in all three cases. The third exercise checks this against the Weyl-group formula and
asks why the group manifold gives nothing.

::: {#exr-cff-families-euler}
#### Families and Euler numbers

Using $\chi(S/R) = |W_S|/|W_R|$ for equal rank and $0$ otherwise, compare the numbers of $\mathbf{27}$s in @prp-cff-nk-fermions with $\tfrac12\chi$, and explain
with @prp-generations-euler why the nearly-Kähler group manifold $SU(2) \times SU(2)$ gives no net family.
:::

::: {.callout-note .solution collapse="true" title="Solution"}
$|W_{G_2}|/|W_{SU(3)}| = 12/6 = 2$, $|W_{Sp(4)}|/|W_{SU(2) \times U(1)}| = 8/2 = 4$, $|W_{SU(3)}|/1 = 6$: half of these are $1, 2, 3$, the numbers of $\mathbf{27}$s
(@exr-vcp-generations-weyl). The group manifold has rank $2 < 3$ for a six-dimensional space, Euler number $0$ (a nowhere-vanishing invariant
vector field exists), and the index $\tfrac12\chi$ of @prp-generations-euler vanishes: any $\mathbf{27}$s come with as many $\overline{\mathbf{27}}$s
(@exr-vcp-nk-rank).
:::

**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.

On a non-symmetric coset the connection used in the reduction has torsion, and the torsion gives the fermions a mass term that
is not a Yukawa coupling. The definition isolates this term.

:::: {.statement-box}
::: {#def-cff-geometric-mass}
#### Geometric fermion mass

On a coset $S/R$ with structure constants $f_{abc}$ in the tangent directions and a connection with contorsion $G_{abc}$, the
reduced fermion Lagrangian contains the **geometric mass term**
$$
\bar\psi V\psi, \qquad V = \tfrac{i}{4}\Gamma^aG_{abc}\Sigma^{bc} ,
$$ {#eq-cff-geometric-mass}
independent of the scalar fields, with $\Sigma^{bc}$ the generators of $SO(6)$ on spinors. On $G_2/SU(3)$, $G_{abc} = \tfrac12(1 - 3\tau)f_{abc}$ with a free
torsion parameter $\tau$, and $V$ is a mass $(1 - 3\tau)\tfrac{6}{\sqrt3}$ (in units of the inverse radius) for the $R$-singlet fermions
[@manousselis2000, eqs. (22), (40)-(41) and Sec. 4].
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
::::

:::: {.callout-note .examples-fold collapse="true" title="Examples"}
The geometric term distinguishes fermions by their $R$-representation. The first example identifies which of the fermions of
@exm-cff-g2su3 receive the mass.

::: {#exm-cff-gaugino-mass}
#### A gaugino mass from geometry

$V$ commutes with the generators of $R$ on spinors and anticommutes with the six-dimensional chirality, so by Schur's lemma it acts
only between the $R$-singlets of $\mathbf 4$ and $\bar{\mathbf 4}$ [@manousselis2000, Sec. 2]. On $G_2/SU(3)$ these are the components that give
the $E_6$ gaugino: the gaugino gets the mass $(1 - 3\tau)\tfrac6{\sqrt3}$, and the fermions in the $\mathbf{27}$ get none. A gaugino mass with massless
matter fermions is a soft breaking of supersymmetry, produced by the geometry.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

On a symmetric coset the structure constants $f_{ab}{}^c$ between tangent directions vanish. The second example states the
consequence for the fermion masses.

::: {#exm-cff-symmetric-no-mass}
#### No geometric mass on symmetric cosets

For $S/R$ symmetric, $[Q_a, Q_b] \subset \mathfrak r$, so $f_{abc} = 0$, the torsion of the canonical connection vanishes, and $V = 0$
[@manousselis2000, Sec. 2]. The geometric mass is a feature of the non-symmetric cosets, the nearly-Kähler ones among them: on the
symmetric $SO(7)/SO(6)$ of @exm-cff-s6-symmetric there is no such term, and the fermion masses come from the Yukawa couplings to the
scalars alone.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::

The geometric mass is part of a linear Dirac operator on a fixed background. The third example shows the other side of the coupling:
a classical spinor field changes the geometry it lives on, which in a compactification it must not do.

::: {#exm-cff-einstein-dirac}
#### The Einstein-Dirac system

The Einstein-Dirac equations $\gamma^a\nabla_a\psi + m\psi = 0$, $R_{ab} - \tfrac12Rg_{ab} = \kappa T_{ab}$, with the energy-momentum tensor of the spinor,
imply $R = \kappa m\psi^+\psi = \kappa m\rho\cos\eta$ in the signature $(+, +, +, -)$ of @zhelnorovich2019spinors [Sec. 6.1, eqs. (6.3)-(6.7)]. On the
homogeneous Bianchi I space $a^2dx^2 + b^2dy^2 + c^2dz^2 - f^2dt^2$, a three-torus with time-dependent radii when $x, y, z$ are periodic, the general
solution has the invariants oscillating with the frequency $2m$ [@zhelnorovich2019spinors, Sec. 6.2, eqs. (6.21)-(6.22)]: a classical spinor
drives the radii. In a vacuum $M^4 \times K$ the spinor fields vanish, since a spinor expectation value would break Lorentz invariance, so the
fermions of this section are fluctuations on a fixed geometry.
:::

::: {.callout-tip .verification collapse="true" title="Verification"}
**Veriphy.** Pending.

**Lean.** Pending.

**Sage.** Pending.
:::
